title: Signs of life: how we tell what is alive

summary.text: A dry moong seed does nothing you can see, while a car zooms, drinks petrol and puffs out smoke. Yet the seed is alive and the car is not. Scientists tell living from non-living things with seven signs, called the life processes: nutrition, respiration, growth, movement, sensing, excretion and reproduction. One sign alone is not enough, because a cloud grows and a car moves. Only living things do all seven, by themselves, over their lives. A dry seed is alive but resting, and in this unit you wake some up and compare them with boiled ones.
summary.art: A child at a table with a magnifying glass, looking at three things in a row: a green moong seed, a toy car and a fluffy cloud drawn on card, with seven small icons floating above them (a plate, a puff of breath, a sprout, running feet, an ear, a drop leaving a leaf, a mother hen with a chick).

intro.hook: Hold a dry moong seed in your palm. The seed does not move, does not eat and does not seem to breathe. Now push a toy car across the floor. It zooms. Which one is alive?
intro.text: Most people say the seed is alive. But ask them why, and it gets hard. The car moves, and the seed does not. A real car even drinks petrol, sucks in air and puffs out smoke. So what does a living thing do that a car never can? Scientists have a list of seven things to look for. In this unit you will test every one of them, on a seed, a cloud and a car.
intro.art: A child's open palm holding one green moong seed, next to a toy car zooming across a tiled floor, with a big question mark between them.

outcomes: I can name the seven life processes and say each in my own words: nutrition, respiration, growth, movement, sensing, excretion and reproduction.
I can test a thing for each sign of life, and fill in a table of what it does and does not do.
I can explain why one sign is not enough to show something is alive, using a seed, a cloud and a car.
I can run a fair test with yeast or seeds, changing only one thing, and then say what I think, what I saw and why.
I can show that plants do all seven life processes, even though they seem to sit still.
I can sort things into alive, once alive and never alive, and give my evidence.
I can link life to energy from the Sun and to atoms that travel between living and non-living things. I can name questions nobody can answer yet, like how life began.

terms.meaning: Something that is alive. Living things feed, grow, sense, make young and do the other signs of life.
terms.example: You, a neem tree, an ant and a mushroom are all living things.
terms.art: A row of four friends: a child, a neem tree, an ant and a mushroom, all smiling in the sun.

terms.meaning: Something that is not alive and never was. It cannot feed, grow from inside or make young.
terms.example: A stone, a steel tumbler, water and air are non-living things.
terms.art: A stone, a steel tumbler, a glass of water and a puff of wind on a windowsill.

terms.meaning: Something that was part of a living thing, but is not alive now.
terms.example: A wooden chair was once a tree. A cotton shirt was once part of a cotton plant. A fallen dry leaf was once alive.
terms.art: A wooden chair with a faint outline of the tree it came from behind it.

terms.meaning: One of the seven jobs every living thing does to stay alive and make more of their kind. We also call them the signs of life.
terms.example: Eating, breathing and growing are three life processes.
terms.art: Seven small picture-icons in a circle: a plate, a puff of breath, a sprout, running feet, an ear, a falling drop and a hen with a chick.

terms.meaning: Getting food. Food gives living things energy and the material to build their bodies. Plants make their own food. Animals eat other living things.
terms.example: A cow eats grass. Tulsi plants make sugar in their leaves using sunlight.
terms.art: A cow chewing grass beside a tulsi plant with sun rays on their leaves.

terms.meaning: The way living things get energy out of their food. It happens inside every tiny part of the body, and it usually uses oxygen from the air.
terms.example: When you run, your body does more respiration, so you breathe faster.
terms.art: A child running, with a zoomed-in circle showing a tiny glowing spark inside the body where food meets air.

terms.meaning: Moving air in and out of the body. Breathing brings in the oxygen that respiration needs. It is not the same as respiration.
terms.example: Your chest goes up and down when you breathe.
terms.art: A child with a hand on their chest, arrows showing air going in and out of the nose.

terms.meaning: Getting bigger and changing, from the inside, by turning food into new body.
terms.example: A puppy grows into a dog. A moong seed grows into a plant.
terms.art: A row showing a moong seed, a sprout, a seedling and a bushy plant.

terms.meaning: Moving the body or a part of it. Animals move from place to place. Plants move slowly, mostly by growing.
terms.example: A dog runs. Young sunflower plants turn their tops to follow the Sun across the sky.
terms.art: A running dog next to a young sunflower plant bending towards the Sun.

terms.meaning: Noticing what is around you and responding to it. Scientists also call it sensitivity.
terms.example: You pull your hand away from a hot pan. The leaves of a touch-me-not plant fold when you touch them.
terms.art: A finger touching a touch-me-not leaf, the little leaflets folding shut.

terms.meaning: Getting rid of waste that the body made inside itself.
terms.example: You breathe out carbon dioxide and you pass wee. Plants give out waste gases through tiny holes in their leaves.
terms.art: A child breathing out a cloud of tiny gas bubbles, next to a leaf with tiny holes letting gas out.

terms.meaning: Making young ones of the same kind.
terms.example: A hen lays eggs. A mango tree makes seeds. A cat has kittens.
terms.art: A hen with eggs, a mango tree with fruit, and a cat with kittens.

terms.meaning: What lets things move, grow, warm up and change. Living things get energy from food.
terms.example: After a good meal you have energy to play.
terms.art: A child jumping high, with a little glowing sun inside their tummy.

terms.meaning: Alive but resting. A dormant thing does almost nothing until the conditions are right.
terms.example: A dry seed is dormant. Water wakes the seed up.
terms.art: A sleeping seed with a tiny nightcap, and a drop of water about to land on the seed.

terms.meaning: To start growing. A seed germinates by waking up and growing a root and a shoot.
terms.example: Moong seeds germinate in a day or two on damp cotton.
terms.art: A moong seed splitting open, a white root poking out and curling down.

terms.meaning: A tiny living building block. Every living thing is made of one or more cells.
terms.example: Your body is made of about 30 million million cells.
terms.art: A wall made of tiny round bricks, with one brick zoomed in to show that the brick is a little living bag.

terms.meaning: A tiny living thing, a kind of fungus, made of just one cell. Bakers use yeast to make bread rise.
terms.example: Dry yeast from a packet wakes up in warm sugar water.
terms.art: A spoon of light brown yeast grains next to a bowl of foamy, bubbling water.

terms.meaning: What you saw, heard or measured that shows something is true.
terms.example: The balloon grew bigger. That is evidence that the yeast made a gas.
terms.art: A child pointing at a puffed-up balloon on a bottle, writing in a notebook.

terms.meaning: A test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same.
terms.example: To test if yeast needs sugar, use the same yeast, water and bottle. Only leave out the sugar.
terms.art: Three identical bottles in a row, only one missing a sugar spoon.

explanations.concept: What it means to be alive: the seven signs
explanations.definition: A living thing belongs to a kind that does all seven life processes: nutrition, respiration, growth, movement, sensing, excretion and reproduction.
explanations.description: Scientists cannot point to one thing that makes something alive. So they use a list of seven signs. Here they are. Nutrition: getting food. Respiration: getting energy from the food. Growth: getting bigger from the inside. Movement: moving the body or a part of it. Sensing: noticing the world and responding. Excretion: getting rid of waste. Reproduction: making young ones. Some children remember them with the made-up word MRS GREN. Each letter starts one sign: Movement, Respiration, Sensing, Growth, Reproduction, Excretion, Nutrition. A living thing does not do all seven at every moment. A child cannot have babies yet, and some animals and people never have young. But every kind of living thing makes more of the same kind.
examples: A dog eats, breathes, grows, runs, sniffs, does wee and can have puppies. That is all seven.
A mango tree makes food in the leaves, takes in air, grows taller, turns the leaves to the light, drops old leaves and grows mangoes with seeds inside.
You do six of the seven every single day. The seventh, having children, can only come when you are grown up.
explanations.art: Seven picture-icons around a smiling child: a plate, a puff of breath, a growing sprout, running feet, an ear, a falling drop and a hen with a chick.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: the seven signs that tell us something is alive.

explanations.concept: Nutrition: every living thing needs food
explanations.definition: Nutrition is how living things get food, for energy and for building their bodies.
explanations.description: All living things need food. Food gives them energy, and it gives them the material to build their bodies. But they get food in different ways. Green plants make their own food. In their leaves, they use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide from the air, and water, into sugar. This is called photosynthesis. Animals cannot do this. They eat plants, or eat animals that ate plants. Mushrooms and other fungi soak up food from dead leaves, wood and soil. So almost all the food in the world started with sunlight caught by plants, or by tiny green living things in the sea.
examples: The leaves of a tulsi plant make sugar when the Sun shines on them.
A goat eats leaves. A tiger eats the goat. Both are getting food that a plant first made.
A mushroom on a rotting log is feeding on the dead wood.
explanations.art: An arrow chain: the Sun shining on a leaf, the leaf eaten by a goat, a mushroom feeding on a fallen log nearby.
explanations.context: This card is about nutrition, the first sign of life: how living things get their food.

explanations.definition: Respiration is how living things get energy out of food, inside their cells. It usually uses oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide.
explanations.description: Many people think respiration means breathing. It does not. Breathing only moves air in and out. Respiration is what happens next, inside every tiny part of your body. There, food and oxygen from the air are joined together. This lets out energy, the way burning does, but slowly and without flames. It also makes carbon dioxide, which you breathe out, and a little water. Plants respire too, all day and all night, in every leaf, stem and root. Even yeast from a packet respires once the yeast wakes up. When you run, your muscles need more energy. So your body does more respiration, and you breathe faster to bring in more oxygen.
examples: When you breathe on a cold mirror, it mists up. Your breath carries water out of your body.
After running, you pant. Your muscles need more oxygen for respiration.
A plant in a dark room keeps respiring, even with no light to make food.
explanations.art: A child breathing in, with a zoomed-in circle inside the arm showing food and oxygen meeting and giving off a little glow of energy.
explanations.context: This card explains respiration, one of the seven signs of life. It is a word many people mix up with breathing.

explanations.concept: Growth: getting bigger from the inside
explanations.definition: Growth is when a living thing gets bigger or changes by turning food into new parts of their own body.
explanations.description: Living things grow from the inside. They take in food and turn it into new parts of their own body. A puppy drinks milk, and part of the milk becomes new puppy body. Non-living things can get bigger too, but only from the outside. A cloud gets bigger when more water vapour in the air cools and turns into drops. A pile of sand gets bigger when you pour more on. Nothing inside the pile is building more pile. Living things also mend and renew themselves. Your skin heals a cut. The red cells in your blood each last about four months, and your body keeps making new ones, millions every second.
examples: A baby grows into a child by turning milk and food into new body.
A cut on your knee heals by itself.
A cloud grows because more water vapour in the air cools and turns into drops, not because the cloud is building itself.
explanations.art: Split picture: on one side a seedling growing taller with arrows coming from inside the stem. On the other side, a cloud getting bigger with arrows coming in from outside.
explanations.context: This card is about growth, one of the seven signs of life, and why a growing cloud is different from a growing child.

explanations.definition: Movement is when a living thing moves their body or part of their body. Animals usually move about. Plants move parts of themselves, mostly by growing.
explanations.description: Animals move from place to place. They walk, swim, fly, crawl and slither. Plants stay in one place, so people think they do not move. But they do, just slowly. Roots grow down into the soil. Shoots bend towards light. Young sunflower plants turn their tops to follow the Sun across the sky. When you touch a touch-me-not plant, their leaves fold in a second. Some plants fold their leaves every night and open them again in the morning. Cars, rivers and wind move too. So movement alone does not prove something is alive.
examples: A money plant on a windowsill leans towards the window.
The touch-me-not plant, called chhui-mui or lajwanti, folds their leaves when touched.
A river moves, but a river is not a living thing. It is full of living things.
explanations.art: A touch-me-not plant with half their leaves folded where a finger touched, and a young sunflower plant bending towards the Sun.
explanations.context: This card is about movement, one of the seven signs of life, and the surprising ways plants move.

explanations.definition: Sensing is when a living thing notices something around them, like light, touch, sound or heat, and responds to it.
explanations.description: Living things notice what is around them, and they respond. You see, hear, smell, taste and touch. When a ball flies at you, you duck. Plants sense too. They sense light, so their shoots grow towards it. They sense which way is down, so roots grow down even in the dark. They sense touch, so a climbing bean curls round a stick. A Venus flytrap plant even counts. The trap snaps shut only when an insect touches the trigger hairs twice in a short time. Even bacteria, with only one cell, swim towards food. Every cell can sense and respond. Plants and bacteria feel, remember and decide in their own way. A root chooses where to grow, and a bacterium decides to swim towards food. Many scientists would call these automatic responses instead.
examples: You blink when dust flies near your eye.
A moong root turns to grow downwards, even if you plant the seed upside down.
A cat's whiskers feel the walls in the dark.
explanations.art: A child ducking a ball, a bean plant curling round a stick, and a Venus flytrap with an ant on the trigger hairs.
explanations.context: This card is about sensing, one of the seven signs of life. It shows that plants and tiny living things sense the world too.

explanations.definition: Excretion is how a living thing gets rid of waste that they made inside their body.
explanations.description: When living things use their food, they make waste. If the waste stayed inside, it would make the body ill. So living things get rid of it. This is called excretion. You breathe out carbon dioxide. Your kidneys clean your blood and make wee. You sweat. Plants give out waste gases through tiny holes in their leaves. In sunlight, one gas they give out is oxygen, the gas we breathe in. Some plants also pack waste into old leaves, and then drop them. Here is a surprise. Poo is mostly water, gut bacteria and food the body could not digest. Scientists call getting rid of it egestion, not excretion. Wee, sweat and breathed-out carbon dioxide are waste the body made itself.
examples: You breathe out carbon dioxide every few seconds.
A tree gives out oxygen as waste from making food, which is lucky for us.
A car gives out smoke from its exhaust pipe. That looks like excretion, but a car is not alive.
explanations.art: A child breathing out, a leaf giving off tiny bubbles of gas, and a car's exhaust puffing smoke, with a question mark over the car.
explanations.context: This card is about excretion, one of the seven signs of life: how living things get rid of the waste they make.

explanations.concept: Reproduction: making more of the same kind
explanations.definition: Reproduction is when a living thing makes young ones of the same kind as the parent.
explanations.description: Every kind of living thing makes young ones. If they did not, that kind would die out. Living things do this in many ways. Many plants make seeds. Hens, snakes and butterflies lay eggs. Cows, cats and people have babies. Some living things just split in two, like bacteria. Yeast grows little buds that break off. A money plant cutting in a bottle of water grows roots and becomes a new plant. The young are always the same kind as the parent. A mango seed never grows into a cat. That is because parents pass on a set of instructions to their young. The instructions are kept inside their cells, in a chemical called DNA.
examples: The aak plant grows on empty plots. Their fluffy seeds blow away in the wind and grow into new aak plants.
A hen's egg hatches into a chick, not a duck.
A cutting of a money plant grows into a whole new plant.
explanations.art: An aak pod bursting with fluffy seeds, a hen with a chick, and a money plant cutting growing roots in a glass bottle.
explanations.context: This card is about reproduction, one of the seven signs of life: how living things make young ones like themselves.

explanations.concept: One sign is not enough: the seed, the cloud and the car
explanations.definition: Something is alive if it does all seven life processes over its life. One or two signs alone are not enough.
explanations.description: To decide if something is alive, scientists do not look at one sign. They look at all seven together. Let us test three things. A car moves. It takes in petrol, a bit like food. It sucks in air and burns the petrol for energy, a bit like respiration. It puffs out smoke, a bit like excretion. Some cars even sense other cars with sensors. But a car never grows, never mends itself and never makes a baby car. People make cars in factories. A cloud moves, and grows, and can split into smaller clouds. But it does not feed or respire, and it only grows when more water vapour in the air cools and turns into drops. A dry seed seems to do almost nothing. But add water and the seed does all seven: feeding on stored food, respiring, growing, moving the root down, sensing which way is down, giving out waste and, one day, making new seeds. So the dry seed is the living one, only resting. Some things are even harder to sort, like fire and viruses. They have their own unit, The edge of life.
examples: A car: moves, takes in fuel and air, gives out smoke, but never grows or reproduces. Not alive.
A cloud: moves, grows and splits, but never feeds, respires or makes young of its own kind. Not alive.
A dry moong seed: shows almost nothing for now, but does all seven once they get water. Alive.
explanations.art: A big table drawn on paper with three columns headed by pictures of a seed, a cloud and a car, and seven rows of ticks and crosses.
explanations.context: This card explains why we test all seven signs of life, not just one, using a seed, a cloud and a car.

explanations.concept: Why living things must keep eating: energy and order
explanations.definition: Living things need a steady flow of energy, mostly from the Sun, to keep their bodies working and in order.
explanations.description: A living body is very well organised, like a busy kitchen where everything is in its place. Keeping it that way takes energy, all the time. A living body uses that energy to keep mending itself. When a living thing dies, the mending stops, and the body slowly breaks down. That is why a dead leaf rots. The energy almost always comes, in the end, from the Sun. A plant catches sunlight and stores it in sugar. A goat eats the plant. You drink the goat's milk. Each time, some energy is used and leaves as warmth. In 1944, the physicist Erwin Schrödinger wrote a famous little book called What Is Life? He said living things stay alive by taking in order from the world around them. Scientists still use that idea today.
examples: You feel warm because respiration in your body gives off heat all the time.
A plant kept in a dark cupboard for weeks uses up their stored food and goes pale and weak.
A fallen leaf, no longer fed by the tree, slowly rots back into soil.
explanations.art: A chain from the Sun to a leaf to a goat to a child, with small wavy warmth lines rising from the goat and the child.
explanations.context: This card goes deeper. It explains why every living thing has to keep taking in food and energy to stay alive.

explanations.concept: Living, once alive and never alive: one world
explanations.definition: Living things are alive now. Once-alive things came from living things. Never-alive things were never part of a living thing.
explanations.description: We can sort things into three groups. Living things are alive now. Once-alive things were part of something alive, like wood, cotton, leather, paper, a fallen leaf or a cooked dal. Never-alive things were never part of a living thing, like stone, steel, glass and water. But the groups are not walled off. The atoms in your body were once in air, water and soil. The carbon in your dal was in the air a year or two ago, before a plant caught it. When a leaf falls and rots, its atoms go back to the soil and air, ready for the next living thing. Everything around us, living and non-living, makes one environment together. Plants need sunlight, water and soil. And living things make soil, change the air and even build rock, like coral reefs.
examples: A wooden table is once alive. It was part of a tree.
A steel spoon is never alive. It was made from rock dug out of the ground.
The water you drink today may once have been inside a fish, a cloud and a mango tree.
explanations.art: Three boxes labelled with pictures: a living ant, a once-alive wooden chair and a never-alive steel spoon, with dotted arrows showing atoms moving between them.
explanations.context: This card is about sorting things into living, once alive and never alive, and how they are all linked.

explanations.concept: Is the line between alive and not alive sharp?
explanations.description: For most things you meet, it is easy to say alive or not alive. A cat is alive. A stone is not. But scientists and thinkers still argue about where the line really is, and whether there is a sharp line at all. Here are some of the main views.
examples: A dry seed can sit for years doing almost nothing, and still be alive.
Fire grows, feeds and spreads, but it is not alive. The unit The edge of life looks at this.
Viruses do nothing on their own, but copy themselves inside a living cell. Scientists still argue about them.

perspectives.who: What the seven signs cannot show
perspectives.explanation: Everything is conscious, living or not, down to the smallest particle. The seven signs show which things scientists call alive. They do not show where awareness begins or ends. So the seven signs are for sorting. They never deny a mind to a stone or a wire.

There is a real line. Living things are made of cells. They take in energy. They pass on instructions to their young, so their kind can slowly change over many generations. Almost everything on Earth falls clearly on one side. Only a few odd cases, like viruses, are hard.

perspectives.who: A group of NASA scientists, in the 1990s
perspectives.explanation: NASA needed to know what to look for on other planets. So a group wrote a working definition. Life is a chemical system that keeps itself going and can change over generations, the way living things on Earth have. It is called a working definition because it is a tool, not the final answer.

perspectives.who: J.C. Bose, an Indian scientist, in 1901 and 1902
perspectives.explanation: Bose tapped metals, plants and animal muscles again and again. He measured their responses with his own instruments. All three got tired, and all three recovered with rest. He wrote that there is no sharp line, only one response running through the living and the non-living. Most scientists today think the metal only looks like it tires, for different reasons. But his plant measurements were real and ahead of their time.

Jain teachings count six kinds of living beings. Plants are one kind. Beings in earth, water, fire and air are four more, and like plants they have one sense, touch. The sixth kind is beings that move about, like animals. This draws the line of life much wider than science does.

explanations.art: A long road that fades gently from a grey stone at one end to a green sprouting seed at the other, with a question mark in the misty middle.
explanations.context: Scientists agree on the seven signs of life. This card is about a harder question: is there a sharp line between alive and not alive?

explanations.description: The oldest signs of life on Earth are more than 3,500 million years old. Before that, there was no life at all. So at some point, non-living chemicals became living things. How did that happen? Nobody knows. Scientists have ideas, and they test them in labs. But nobody has yet made a living thing from plain chemicals.
examples: In 1871, Charles Darwin wrote in a letter that life might have started in a 'warm little pond' full of chemicals.
In 1952, Stanley Miller, a young American student, sent sparks like lightning through a jar of gases and water. After some days he found building blocks of living things in the water.
Some scientists think life began in hot springs on the deep sea floor, where warm, chemical-rich water bubbles out of rock.

perspectives.explanation: Life began in small pools on land, where chemicals were dried by the Sun and wetted by rain, again and again, until they joined into long chains.
Life began deep in the sea, at hot springs in the rock. There, energy and chemicals are always flowing, like a natural battery.
Before cells, there may have been a chemical that could both carry instructions and copy itself, called RNA. Cells came later. Many scientists like this idea, but it is still being tested.

explanations.art: A young Earth: a steaming pond under a lightning-filled sky on one side, and a deep-sea hot spring puffing black smoke on the other.
explanations.context: This card is about one of the biggest unanswered questions in science: how the first living thing came from non-living things.

agreed.text: Every kind of living thing we know does all seven life processes.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have named about two million kinds of living things, from bacteria to blue whales. All of them feed, respire, grow, sense, get rid of waste and reproduce, and all move in some way.

agreed.text: All living things are made of cells.
agreed.evidence: Robert Hooke first saw cells through a microscope in 1665. Since then, every living thing examined has turned out to be made of one or more cells. Two German scientists, Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann, put this together as the cell theory in 1838 and 1839.

agreed.text: Today, living things only come from other living things.
agreed.evidence: In the 1860s, Louis Pasteur, a French scientist, boiled soup in flasks with long curved necks. Air could get in, but dust and tiny living things got stuck in the curved neck. The soup stayed clear and nothing grew. When he broke the neck off, the soup soon went cloudy with life.

agreed.text: Plants are alive, and they sense and respond.
agreed.evidence: Plants grow towards light, send roots down, fold leaves when touched and send electrical signals through their bodies. J.C. Bose measured some of these signals over 100 years ago, and modern instruments confirm them.

agreed.text: All living things on Earth are related.
agreed.evidence: Every living thing uses the same kind of instructions, written in a chemical called DNA, and the same code to read them. The best explanation is that all life comes from one shared ancestor long ago.

challenging.claim: Things that move are alive. Things that do not move are not.
challenging.who: Many young children, and many grown-ups without noticing. In the 1920s, Jean Piaget, a Swiss psychologist, found that young children often call the Sun, the wind and bicycles alive, because they move.
challenging.for: It matches what we see. Animals, the things we know best as alive, are always moving.
challenging.against: Cars, rivers and wind move, and are not alive. Trees and dry seeds hardly move, and are alive. Movement is only one of seven signs.
challenging.context: This card is about a very common idea of what makes something alive, and why it does not work.

challenging.claim: Plants are less alive than animals.
challenging.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker about 2,350 years ago, said plants have only a feeding and growing kind of life, with no feeling. Many people still feel this.
challenging.for: Plants have no eyes, ears, brains or nerves. They do not run from danger.
challenging.against: Plants do all seven signs of life. They sense light, gravity and touch. J.C. Bose showed plants send electrical signals when hurt. In 1880, Charles Darwin and his son Francis wrote a whole book on how plants move. Plants feel, in their own way, without nerves.
challenging.context: This card is about the old idea that plants are less alive than animals.

challenging.claim: Living things contain a special life force that non-living things lack.
challenging.who: This idea is called vitalism. Many scientists believed it until the 1800s.
challenging.for: Living things seem so different from stones and water. It feels as if something extra must be inside them.
challenging.against: Scientists found that living things are made of ordinary atoms, the same ones in air and rock. In 1897, Eduard Buchner, a German scientist, crushed yeast cells and used just their juice. It still turned sugar into gas, with no living cells at all. He won a Nobel Prize for it in 1907.
challenging.context: This card is about the old idea of a life force, and what yeast showed about it.

challenging.claim: The whole Earth behaves like one living thing.
challenging.who: James Lovelock, a British scientist, in the 1970s, with the American biologist Lynn Margulis. They called it the Gaia idea, after a Greek name for the Earth.
challenging.for: Living things change the air, the seas and the rocks. Those changes help keep Earth fit for life, a bit like a body keeps itself warm.
challenging.against: The Earth does not reproduce or pass on instructions, so most scientists say it is not alive. Many agree that life and the Earth are tightly linked, and they study them together as one system.
challenging.context: This card is about a big idea: could the whole Earth be a kind of living thing?

challenging.claim: There is no sharp line between living and non-living. The same response runs through both.
challenging.who: J.C. Bose, an Indian scientist in Calcutta, in his 1902 book Response in the Living and Non-Living.
challenging.for: He measured how metals, plants and muscles responded when tapped again and again. Their records looked alike. All tired, and all recovered after rest.
challenging.against: Most scientists say the metal only looks as if it tires, for different reasons that have nothing to do with life. A metal does not feed, grow or reproduce.
challenging.context: This card is about J.C. Bose's daring idea that living and non-living things are not so different.

challenging.who: Monica Gagliano, an Australian scientist, and her team, in 2014. They dropped touch-me-not plants a short, harmless distance again and again.
challenging.for: At first the plants folded their leaves each time. After many drops, they stopped folding. Weeks later, they still did not fold when dropped. But they still folded when shaken in a new way. So the plants learned that the drop was safe, and remembered it.
challenging.against: Other scientists say the plants may just have been tired, or their sense of touch may have gone dull. Some say the words learning and memory should be kept for animals with brains. They want the test repeated by other teams.
challenging.context: This card is about a new and argued idea: can a plant learn?

big_questions.q: Is a dry seed in a packet alive right now, or only alive later?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens when you boil a seed. A boiled seed never wakes up. So what was in the dry seed that the boiled seed lost?

big_questions.q: Why does a car need a factory, but a hen does not need a factory to make a chick?
big_questions.hint: Where are the instructions for making a chick kept? Where are the instructions for a car kept?

big_questions.q: If you breathe out, and a tree takes in your breath to make sugar, and you eat a mango from that tree, where do you end and the tree begin?
big_questions.hint: Follow one atom of carbon on its journey.

big_questions.q: Is your body the same body you had last year?
big_questions.hint: Many of your cells have been replaced since then. Your blood cells last only about four months.

big_questions.q: If we found something on Mars, how would we know if it was alive?
big_questions.hint: Which of the seven signs could a robot test from far away?

big_questions.q: Could something be a little bit alive?
big_questions.hint: Think of a dry seed, a virus, or J.C. Bose's tired metal. Is alive a switch, or more like a dimmer?

big_questions.q: Does a plant feel your touch?
big_questions.hint: Plants do, in their own way. A touch-me-not senses and responds. How could we find out what the touch is like for the plant?

big_questions.q: Why do living things die, when a stone can last for millions of years?
big_questions.hint: What does a living thing have to keep doing that a stone does not?

big_questions.q: Why do we care more about hurting a dog than a stone? What about hurting a plant?
big_questions.hint: Jain teachings say even earth and water hold life. How would that change how you treat them?

big_questions.q: Is a river alive? In 2017 a court in Uttarakhand said the Ganga and Yamuna should be treated as living persons. India's Supreme Court later put this on hold.
big_questions.hint: Check the seven signs. Then ask: what changes if we treat a river as if it were alive?

big_questions.q: Where did the very first living thing come from?
big_questions.hint: Life today comes only from life. But there was a time with no life on Earth at all.

story.title: The Girl Who Tapped the Shy Plant
story.note: J.C. Bose was real, and he worked at Presidency College in Calcutta. He really did compare the 'tiring' of metals, plants and muscles, and published Response in the Living and Non-Living in 1902. His studies of the touch-me-not plant came a few years later than this story. He really did refuse his reduced pay for about three years. Tuli, her mother and Haren are made up, and the instruments are simplified.
text: In the year 1902, in the city of Calcutta, there was a room in Presidency College that smelled of candle smoke and wet earth. Tuli knew that smell better than anyone. Her mother swept that room every evening, and Tuli, who was ten, carried her bucket.

The room belonged to Professor Jagadish Chandra Bose. People whispered about him. He was an Indian professor in a college run by the British, and they had once paid him less than the English teachers. So for three whole years he had refused to take any pay at all. Tuli thought that was either very brave or very foolish. She had not decided which.

The professor's tables were covered in strange things. Coils of wire. Glass plates blackened with smoke. Needles so fine you could hardly see them. And in the middle of it all, in a cracked clay pot, sat a small, scruffy plant with feathery leaves. Tuli knew that plant. They grew wild beside the railway line. Everyone called them lajwanti, the shy one, because when you touched them, their leaves folded shut, as if they were embarrassed.

One evening, the professor looked up from his work. 'You,' he said to Tuli. 'You have steady hands. Would you like a job?' The job was simple. Every time the big clock ticked round a minute, Tuli had to touch one leaf of the shy plant with a feather. Then she had to tap a thin metal wire, clamped on the other table, with a little brass hammer. The professor's machines would record what happened.

Haren, the professor's young assistant, rolled his eyes. 'Sir is wasting his time,' he whispered, once the professor had gone into the next room. 'A plant is a green thing. A wire is a grey thing. Neither of them feels anything. Tap away.'

So Tuli tapped. Feather on leaf. Hammer on wire. Feather on leaf. Hammer on wire. At first the shy plant folded fast, their little leaflets snapping together like hands at prayer, and a needle drew a tall line on the smoked glass. For the wire, a spot of light jumped along a scale on the wall. But after twenty taps, something changed. The plant folded more slowly. The plant's lines grew shorter. And the spot of light from the wire jumped less, too.
'They are both getting tired,' said the professor softly, when he came back. He held the two records side by side. They looked almost the same.

Haren laughed. 'There you are, sir. Same, same. The plant is just a thing, like the wire.' The professor only said, 'How do you know what a plant feels, Haren? Or a wire? Let them rest. We will try again tomorrow.'

That night Tuli could not sleep. She lay on her mat and thought about the shy plant, sitting in the dark in their cracked pot. If Haren was right, the plant was no different from the wire. Then why had it felt wrong to keep tapping the plant? She had not minded tapping the wire at all.
She came back early the next morning, before her mother, before anyone. She let herself into the smoky room, stood very still, and watched.

The wire lay on the table exactly as she had left it. Not one bit of it had changed. But the plant had. In the night, all of their leaves had folded down and drooped, though nobody had touched them. Now, as the first light came through the high window, they were opening again, slowly, all on their own. The soil in the pot, which had been damp, was dry. The plant had drunk the water. Their leaves were tilted towards the window. At the tip of one stem, where yesterday there had been a tight green knot, a new leaf was uncurling. And under the leaves hung a fluffy pink ball, like a tiny sweet. A flower. Flowers make seeds, her mother always said. Seeds make new plants.
Tuli looked back at the wire. It had not drunk anything. It had not grown. It had not turned to the light. It would never make a little wire. It just lay there, waiting for someone to hit it.
She poured water into the pot, slowly, the way her mother watered the tulsi at home. Then she sat on the floor and watched the plant go on doing all their quiet work, with nobody to make them.

When the professor came in, Tuli jumped up. 'Sir, they are not the same!' The words tumbled out. 'The wire only does something when I hit it. The plant does things by themselves. They drink. They sleep at night and wake up in the morning. They turn to the window. They are growing a new leaf. They have a flower, for seeds. The wire does nothing until somebody does something to it.'
Haren, who had followed the professor in, opened his mouth and shut it again.

The professor sat down on a stool, so that his eyes were level with Tuli's. 'You have watched well,' he said. 'Better than many men with degrees. The plant feeds, grows, moves and makes seeds. They do all of it from inside themselves. That is what living things do.' Then he picked up the two smoky glass plates and held them to the light. 'And yet, look. When we tap them, both grow tired. When they rest, both recover. In this one way, the wire and the plant are alike.'
'So which is it, sir?' asked Tuli. 'Is the wire a little bit alive? Or is the plant a little bit like a wire?'

The professor laughed, a big, surprised laugh. 'Now you have asked my question,' he said. 'Where is the line, Tuli? Did nature draw it? Or did we?' He did not answer it. He handed Tuli the feather instead. 'Today,' he said, 'you will let the plant rest for a whole hour between taps. Then we will see what a living thing does with rest.'

Tuli took the feather. Before she began, she touched the shy plant, very gently, with one finger. Their leaflets folded shut. Then, after a while, slowly, as if they had made up their mind, they opened again.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the wire and the plant share one sign of life, responding when touched, and both even tire and recover. But only the plant does everything else, by themselves and from inside: they drink, grow, move to the light, sleep and wake, and make flowers for seeds. One sign is not enough to call something alive. All the signs together are. The story also leaves Bose's real question open: is the line between living and non-living drawn by nature, or by us? And it quietly asks who gets noticed: a cleaner's daughter, and an Indian scientist paid less than his colleagues.
ask: In the story, the plant and the wire both got tired when tapped. So why did Tuli say they were not the same?
What did the plant do in the night, when nobody was touching them?
Which signs of life did Tuli spot in the plant? Can you name four?
The professor asked, 'Did nature draw the line, or did we?' What do you think?
Haren thought the plant could not feel anything. Tuli felt it was wrong to keep tapping the plant. Who do you agree with, and why?

games.title: Life Trial: Alive, Once Alive or Never Alive?
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the app
games.context: This is a card game about the seven signs of life. Players put everyday things on trial. For each thing, they decide which signs it shows, then whether it is alive, once alive or never alive.

printables.title: 24 thing cards to cut out
items: A money plant cutting in a bottle

printables.title: 7 sign cards for each player
items: M: Movement (moves their body or parts of it)
E: Excretion (gets rid of their own waste)
R: Reproduction (makes young of their kind)

rules: Cut out the 24 thing cards. Shuffle them and put them face down.
Each player takes a set of 7 sign cards.
On your turn, turn over a thing card and read it out loud.
Everyone holds up the sign cards they think this thing really shows, at some time in its life.
The player whose turn it is gives the verdict: alive, once alive or never alive. They put the card on that mat and say why.
Score 1 point for each sign you can explain. Score 2 points for a verdict with a good reason. If someone challenges you with good evidence, they win the 2 points instead.
Remember the big rule: one sign is not enough. A living thing does all seven over its life.
When the cards run out, the player with the most points wins.

setup.art: Three paper mats on a floor, labelled with a green sprout, a brown leaf and a grey stone, with a pile of face-down picture cards beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the three mats: ALIVE, ONCE ALIVE and NEVER ALIVE.

setup.art: A child holding up three small cards with a running-feet icon, a plate icon and a smoke-puff icon, looking at a card showing a car.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over a thing. Everyone holds up the signs it shows.

setup.art: A child placing a car card on the grey stone mat while two others nod.
setup.caption: 3. Give the verdict, put the card on a mat, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the three mats. 2. Shuffle the thing cards and put them face down. 3. Give each player 7 sign cards.
flow.say: Every card is a thing from everyday life. We are going to put each one on trial. Is it alive, once alive, or never alive? But first we check which of the seven signs of life it shows.
flow.kid: Put out the three mats. Mix up the thing cards. Take your 7 sign cards. For each thing, you check its signs. Then you decide.
flow.context: This is the first step of Life Trial. It is a card game about the seven signs of life. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Find the card 'A car'. Play it together as a practice round.
flow.say: Let's practise with the car. Hold up every sign a car shows. Think about a real car on the road.
flow.kid: Practice card: a car. Which signs of life does it show? Hold them up.

ask.q: Which signs does a car seem to show?
good: It takes in petrol, like food.
It sucks in air and burns the petrol.

check.q: A car moves, drinks fuel and puffs out smoke. Which two signs of life can a car never do?
options: Move and sense
Grow and make young
Take in fuel and give out smoke
check.why: A car never grows bigger by itself, and it never makes a baby car. People build cars in factories. So even though a car seems to show some signs, it is never alive. Picking 'move and sense' usually means forgetting that cars do move, and modern cars have sensors. Picking 'fuel and smoke' means missing that these look a lot like eating and getting rid of waste.

flow.parent: A car can look like it does up to five signs. That is the point of the game. Praise your child for spotting them, then ask about growth and young ones.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Each player turns over a card and reads it out. 2. Everyone holds up signs. 3. The player gives a verdict and a reason. 4. Keep score on the score sheet.
flow.say: When you give your verdict, tell us your evidence. Which signs does it show? Which is it missing?
flow.kid: Take turns. Turn over a card. Hold up its signs. Then choose: alive, once alive or never alive. Say why.
flow.parent: Tricky cards on purpose. Yeast is alive, a fungus made of one cell. A coral reef is built by tiny living animals, so a living reef is alive, but its rocky skeleton is once alive. A money plant cutting is alive. Bread and a cotton shirt are once alive. Wind, a river, a soap bubble and a light bulb are never alive, though they move or grow or glow. A mobile phone senses touch and needs charging, but it never grows or makes young. A ripe mango is still alive: the cells keep respiring, and the seed can grow a tree. A hen's egg from a shop will never hatch, because no chick is growing in it. So many people put it on once alive. An egg that a hen sits on can be alive, with a chick growing inside.

flow.do: When someone draws 'A dry moong seed', stop and talk about it.
flow.say: A dry seed does almost nothing right now. So how can they be alive?
flow.kid: A dry seed! Almost nothing is happening. Is the seed alive?

check.q: A dry moong seed seems to do nothing. Why do we still call the seed alive?
options: Because they are small and green
Because, with water, they wake up and do all seven signs
Because they came from a shop
check.why: A dry seed is dormant. They are alive but resting. Give the seed water and warmth, and they feed on their stored food, respire, grow a root, sense which way is down and later make new seeds. Picking 'small and green' means judging by looks. A green bead is small and green too, and it is not alive.

flow.do: Count the points. Then look at the three mats together.
flow.say: Look at the ALIVE mat. What do all these things have in common?
flow.kid: Count your points. Look at the ALIVE mat. What do they all do?
flow.think: Is there a card you are still not sure about? Keep it to one side. Scientists have cards like that too.

games.title: MRS GREN Moves
games.players: 1 or more children and a caller
games.context: This is a quick action game to remember the seven signs of life. The caller shouts a sign, and everyone acts it out. MRS GREN is a memory name: each letter starts one sign of life.

printables.title: 7 action cards
items: M for Movement: walk like an elephant
R for Respiration: take three big slow breaths
S for Sensing: freeze and listen like a deer
G for Growth: grow from a tiny crouch to tall
R for Reproduction: rock a baby in your arms
E for Excretion: breathe out a long whoosh
N for Nutrition: munch like a goat

rules: The caller shuffles the action cards and calls one out.
Everyone acts it out at once.
In round two, the caller calls a sign and a living-thing card together, for example, 'Movement: a neem tree!'
Players act out how that living thing does that sign, and say it in one sentence.
Anyone can call 'Challenge!' if they think the action is wrong.

setup.art: A parent holding up a card with an elephant picture while two children stomp like elephants.
setup.caption: 1. The caller holds up a sign card. Everyone acts it out.

setup.art: A child standing still with arms out wide like branches, slowly turning their face towards a lamp, as a parent holds a tree card.
setup.caption: 2. In round two, act out how a living thing does that sign.

flow.do: Call out all seven action cards, one by one. Everyone acts each one.
flow.say: MRS GREN helps us remember the seven signs of life. Each letter starts one sign. Ready? M! Walk like an elephant. That's Movement.
flow.kid: Listen to the caller. Act out each sign. M is for Movement. Walk like an elephant!
flow.context: This is MRS GREN Moves, a quick game to remember the seven signs of life by acting them out.

flow.do: Call a sign together with a living-thing card. For example, 'Movement: a neem tree!'
flow.say: Now it's harder. Movement, a neem tree! How does a tree move? Show me, and tell me in one sentence.
flow.kid: Now the caller says a sign and a living thing. Show how they do that sign. Say it in one sentence.

ask.q: How does a neem tree move?
good: Their branches grow towards the light.
Their leaves sway, but that is the wind. They move themselves by growing.

check.q: Excretion: a neem tree! How does a tree get rid of their waste?
options: They cannot. Trees make no waste.
They give out waste gases through tiny holes in their leaves, and drop old leaves.
They push waste out of their roots like a tap.
check.why: Trees make waste, like every living thing. They give out waste gases through tiny holes in their leaves, and they drop old leaves with some waste stored inside. Picking 'trees make no waste' usually means thinking only animals do excretion.

flow.do: End by calling all seven very fast, in MRS GREN order.
flow.say: Last round, super fast. M, R, S, G, R, E, N!
flow.kid: Last round! Act all seven, fast as you can.
flow.think: Which of the seven did you do today, without even trying?

experiments.title: The Balloon Test: is something alive in the yeast packet?
experiments.question: Is the dry yeast in a packet alive? And what does yeast need to show signs of life?
experiments.predict: Before you start, look at the three bottles. Bottle A gets yeast, sugar and warm water. Bottle B gets yeast and warm water, but no sugar. Bottle C gets yeast, sugar and cold water from the fridge. Which balloon do you think will grow the most? Which will grow the least? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same size bottles, the same balloons, the same spoon of yeast and the same amount of water. Change only one thing in each bottle: the sugar or the warmth. Start all three at the same time and measure them at the same time.
results_table: Distance round the flat balloon at the start (cm)
Distance round the balloon after 30 minutes (cm)

materials.item: 3 empty plastic water bottles, all the same size (half-litre bottles work well)
3 balloons, all the same
dry yeast (instant or active), 6 teaspoons
sugar, 2 tablespoons
warm water, 1 cup (as warm as a bath, not hot)
cold water from the fridge, half a cup
a piece of string and a ruler, or a tailor's tape
a funnel or a rolled-up paper cone

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the warm water. It should feel like a warm bath on the inside of your wrist, never hot. Do not drink the mixture. Pull the balloons off over a sink, away from faces.

schedule.what: Guess which balloon will grow most. Set up the three bottles. Watch for 30 minutes. Measure the balloons and draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for each bottle. Make each bar as tall as the distance round its balloon.
experiments.context: This is the balloon test. You put dry yeast into three bottles with different mixtures, and stretch a balloon over each. If the yeast is alive, they will feed, respire and give out a gas that blows up the balloon.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: distance round each balloon after 30 minutes
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Each flat balloon measured 12 cm round at the start. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Three small plastic bottles in a row labelled A, B and C, with a spoon of yeast going into each through a paper funnel.
setup.caption: 1. Put two teaspoons of yeast in each bottle. Add sugar to A and C only.

setup.art: A grown-up pouring warm water into bottles A and B, and a child pouring cold water from a fridge bottle into bottle C.
setup.caption: 2. Add warm water to A and B, and fridge-cold water to C. Swirl each one.

setup.art: Three bottles with balloons stretched over their necks: A's balloon standing up fat, B's a little floppy, C's flat.
setup.caption: 3. Stretch a balloon over each neck. Wait 30 minutes and watch.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the dry yeast. 2. Let them feel and smell the yeast. 3. Ask whether they think the yeast is alive.
flow.say: This is yeast. Bakers use yeast to make bread soft and puffy. Does yeast look alive to you? No moving, eating or growing. Let's test.
flow.kid: Look at the yeast. Feel and smell the yeast. Does yeast look alive? We are going to find out.

ask.q: How could we find out if this yeast is alive?
good: Give the yeast food and see what happens.

flow.context: This is the first step of the balloon test. You find out if dry yeast is alive by giving the yeast food and warmth, and watching for signs of life.

flow.do: 1. Label the bottles A, B and C. 2. Ask your child to guess which balloon will grow most and least. 3. Write the guess down.
flow.say: Bottle A gets yeast, sugar and warm water. B gets yeast and warm water, but no sugar. C gets yeast, sugar and cold water. Which balloon will grow most? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A gets yeast, sugar and warm water. B gets no sugar. C gets cold water. Which balloon will grow most? Why? Write your guess.

flow.do: 1. Wrap the string round each flat balloon and write the length in the table. 2. Put two teaspoons of yeast in each bottle, using a funnel. 3. Add one tablespoon of sugar to A and to C. Add none to B. 4. A grown-up pours half a cup of warm water into A and into B. 5. Pour half a cup of fridge-cold water into C. 6. Swirl each bottle. 7. Stretch a balloon over each neck. Blow each balloon up and let it down two or three times first, so it stretches easily.
flow.say: We change only one thing in each bottle, so the test is fair. Now let's stretch on the balloons. If anything in there is alive and gives out a gas, the balloon will catch it.
flow.kid: Measure each flat balloon. Yeast in all three. Sugar in A and C. Warm water in A and B. Cold water in C. Swirl. Put a balloon on each.
flow.parent: The warm water should feel like a bath on the inside of your wrist, around 40 degrees. Hot water will kill the yeast. If nothing happens in bottle A after 20 minutes, your yeast may be old. Check the date on the packet, and try a fresh one. Keep an opened packet closed tight in the fridge.

flow.do: 1. Watch for 10 minutes. 2. Look for bubbles and foam in each bottle. 3. Then wait until 30 minutes have passed.
flow.say: Look at bottle A. Can you see bubbles? Foam? Now look at B and C. What do you think the bubbles are? Where do you think they come from?
flow.kid: Watch the bottles. Do you see bubbles or foam? What do you think made them? Wait until 30 minutes are up.
flow.parent: Bottle A should foam, and its balloon should start to stand up within 10 to 20 minutes. Bottle B may make a little gas. Bottle C stays almost still, because the cold slows the yeast right down. The gas is carbon dioxide, a waste the yeast gives out while getting energy from sugar. The yeast is also growing and making new yeast cells by budding, which is too small to see. If balloon A is still small at 30 minutes, wait 15 minutes more.

check.q: In the balloon test, bottle A is foaming and its balloon is filling up. What is happening?
options: The water is boiling
The yeast is feeding on sugar and giving out a gas
The sugar is melting into air
check.why: Yeast is alive. The yeast feeds on the sugar, gets energy from it and gives out carbon dioxide gas as waste. The gas fills the balloon. That is nutrition, respiration and excretion, three signs of life. Picking 'boiling' means mixing up bubbles from heat with bubbles from life. The water is only warm. Picking 'sugar melting into air' means thinking sugar turns into gas by itself. It does not, or bottle C would fill too.

flow.do: 1. After 30 minutes, wrap a string round the fattest part of each balloon. 2. Lay the string on a ruler to read the length. 3. Write it in the table. 4. Draw a bar for each bottle.
flow.say: Let's measure. The bigger the distance round the balloon, the more gas the yeast made. Each bottle gets one bar.
flow.kid: Wrap the string round each balloon. Measure it with a ruler. Write it down. Draw one bar for each bottle.

chart.title: Made-up example results: distance round each balloon after 30 minutes
chart.note: Made-up numbers to show the idea. Each flat balloon was 12 cm round at the start. Yours will be different.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. Is the yeast alive? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: yeast is alive, and needs food and warmth. What I saw: all three balloons started at 12 cm round. Balloon A grew to 30 cm, but B only reached 14 cm and C 13 cm. Why: the yeast fed on the sugar and gave out gas as waste. In the cold, the yeast was too slow. Without sugar, there was almost no food.
flow.think: Bakers knead yeast into dough and leave it somewhere warm. Why warm? What would happen in the fridge?

experiments.title: Sleeping or dead? The seed test
experiments.question: Is a dry seed alive? How can we tell a sleeping seed from a dead one?
experiments.predict: Before you start, look at the four cups. Cup A has soaked seeds on wet cotton. Cup B has dry seeds on dry cotton. Cup C has boiled seeds on wet cotton. Cup D has plastic beads on wet cotton. In which cups will something grow? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use 5 seeds or beads in each cup, the same cotton, the same amount of water and the same warm place. Change only one thing: wet or dry, boiled or not, seed or bead. Check all four cups at the same time each day.

materials.item: 15 whole green moong seeds from a recent packet, and a few spare (split moong dal will not sprout)
5 small plastic beads or buttons, about the size of a seed
4 small cups or steel bowls
cotton wool
a small pan to boil 5 seeds, for a grown-up
a ruler
a magnifying glass, if you have one

experiments.safety: A grown-up boils the seeds and lets them cool. Wash your hands after touching the seeds.

schedule.what: Soak 5 seeds overnight. A grown-up boils 5 more for 10 minutes. Guess which cups will grow.
Set up all four cups. Count and draw.
Count how many have sprouted in each cup. Keep A, C and D damp.
Count again. Look at the roots with a magnifying glass.
Count again. Move the dry seeds from cup B onto wet cotton.
Measure the longest root in each cup. Did cup B wake up? Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Each day, write how many of the 5 have sprouted in each cup. On the last day, measure the longest root in each cup.
experiments.context: This is the seed test. You put moong seeds and plastic beads in four cups, some wet, some dry, some boiled. Then you watch which ones wake up and grow.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how many of 5 sprouted by day 4
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Four small steel bowls in a row labelled A, B, C and D, each with a bed of cotton wool: A with plump soaked seeds, B with dry seeds, C with soft boiled seeds, D with small plastic beads.
setup.caption: 1. Set up four cups: soaked seeds, dry seeds, boiled seeds and beads.

setup.art: A child gently dripping water from a spoon onto the cotton in cups A, C and D, leaving B dry.
setup.caption: 2. Keep A, C and D damp each day. Keep B dry.

setup.art: Cup A full of moong sprouts with long white roots curling down, the other cups unchanged, and a ruler beside cup A.
setup.caption: 3. Count the sprouts each day. Measure the longest root.

flow.do: 1. Count out 5 moong seeds and soak them in water overnight. 2. A grown-up boils 5 more seeds for 10 minutes, then lets them cool. 3. Keep 5 dry seeds aside. 4. Find 5 small plastic beads or buttons.
flow.say: Here are seeds and beads. Which ones are alive? It's hard to tell just by looking. So let's give them water and wait.
flow.kid: Soak 5 seeds overnight. A grown-up boils 5 other seeds. Keep 5 seeds dry. Find 5 beads.
flow.context: This is the first step of the seed test. You find out if dry seeds are alive by watching which ones wake up.

flow.do: 1. Put cotton in four cups. Label them A, B, C and D. 2. A: soaked seeds, wet cotton. B: dry seeds, dry cotton. C: boiled seeds, wet cotton. D: beads, wet cotton. 3. Put the cups somewhere warm, out of direct sun.
flow.say: We changed only one thing in each cup. Now, which ones do you think will grow?
flow.kid: Set up the four cups. A: soaked seeds. B: dry seeds. C: boiled seeds. D: beads. Make A, C and D wet.

ask.q: Which cups do you think will grow? Why?
good: A, because the seeds have water.
Not D, because beads were never alive.
Not C, because boiling may kill the baby plant.

flow.do: Each day, count the sprouted seeds in each cup and write the numbers in the table. Keep A, C and D damp. Look at the roots with a magnifying glass.
flow.say: Look, cup A has white roots poking out! Which way are they growing? Let's count how many have sprouted.
flow.kid: Count the sprouts in each cup. Write the numbers. Look at a root with a magnifying glass. Which way does it grow?
flow.wait: Do this once a day, on days 3, 4 and 5.
flow.parent: Moong usually sprouts within one or two days. In a cold room it can take three or four, so keep the cups somewhere warm, like a kitchen shelf. The roots always turn to grow downwards. That is the seed sensing gravity and moving by growing. If a few seeds in A do not sprout, that is normal. Not every seed is healthy. The boiled seeds may grow a fuzzy mould after a few days. The mould is a different living thing, a fungus, feeding on the dead seeds.

flow.do: On day 5, move the dry seeds from cup B onto wet cotton.
flow.say: Cup B's seeds have been dry all this time. Are they dead, or just sleeping? Let's give them water and see.
flow.kid: Move the dry seeds from cup B onto wet cotton. Are they dead, or just sleeping?
flow.parent: The dry seeds will swell overnight. In warm weather, many show a root tip by the next day. If they have only swollen, wait one more day.

flow.do: On day 6, measure the longest root in each cup and write it down.
flow.say: Let's measure. What happened in each cup?
flow.kid: Measure the longest root in each cup. Write it down.

check.q: In the seed test, the boiled seeds on wet cotton never sprouted, but the dry seeds sprouted once they got water. What does this show?
options: Dry seeds are dead, and water brings them back to life
Dry seeds are alive but resting. Boiling killed the seeds.
Boiled seeds need more water than other seeds
check.why: A dry seed is dormant: alive but resting. Water wakes the seed up. Boiling destroyed the living baby plant inside, so those seeds can never grow. Picking 'water brings dead seeds back to life' means thinking the dry seeds were dead. But the boiled seeds had water too, and they did not grow. Picking 'boiled seeds need more water' misses that cup C had just as much water as cup A.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences: what I think, what I saw and why.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. Is a dry seed alive? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a dry seed is alive, but resting. What I saw: all 5 soaked seeds sprouted, and the dry seeds sprouted after I gave them water. The boiled seeds and the beads never grew. Why: the seed has a living baby plant inside. Water wakes them up. Boiling kills them, and beads were never alive.

experiments.title: Breath Counter: does moving need more energy?
experiments.question: When you move fast, does your body need more air? What does that tell us about respiration?
experiments.predict: Guess how many breaths you take in one minute sitting still. Then guess how many after one minute of jumping. Why do you think it will change?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, the same person counts in the same way each time, for the same 15 seconds. Sit still for two minutes before the first count. Do each count three times and take the middle number.

materials.item: a clock or phone with a seconds timer
a pencil and the results table
a hand mirror, for an extra test

experiments.safety: Jump on a soft, flat floor. Stop if you feel dizzy or your chest hurts. A child with asthma can march on the spot gently instead.

schedule.what: Count breaths sitting still, then after jumping, then after resting. Turn the counts into breaths per minute and draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart with three bars: sitting still, just after jumping and after two minutes of rest.
experiments.context: This is the breath counter. You count how many breaths you take sitting still and after jumping. It shows that your body needs more oxygen for respiration when your muscles work hard.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: breaths in one minute
example_chart.note: Made-up numbers to show the idea. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A child sitting cross-legged with one hand on their tummy, a parent watching a phone timer.
setup.caption: 1. Sit still for 2 minutes. Count breaths for 15 seconds.

setup.art: A child doing star jumps on a rug, red-cheeked and puffing.
setup.caption: 2. Jump for 1 minute. Count breaths for 15 seconds again.

setup.art: A child sitting down again, breathing slower, writing numbers in a table.
setup.caption: 3. Rest for 2 minutes. Count once more.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits still for 2 minutes. 2. They put a hand on their tummy. 3. Time 15 seconds while they count each breath in. 4. Do it three times. Write the numbers.
flow.say: Put a hand on your tummy. Each time it goes out, that is one breath in. I'll say go and stop. You count.
flow.kid: Sit still. Hand on tummy. Count each breath in until the grown-up says stop.
flow.context: This is the first step of the breath counter. You count your breaths sitting still, so you can compare them with breaths after jumping.

flow.do: 1. Your child jumps on the spot for 1 minute. 2. Straight away, count their breaths for 15 seconds. 3. Write the number. Rest and repeat twice more, if they are happy to.
flow.say: Now jump for one whole minute. Go! Stop. Quick, count your breaths.
flow.kid: Jump for one minute. Stop. Count your breaths straight away.
flow.parent: Most children breathe about twice as fast after jumping. Their heart beats faster too. Let them feel their heartbeat with two fingers on the side of the neck.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits still for 2 minutes. 2. Count breaths again for 15 seconds.
flow.say: Rest now. Is your breathing slowing down? Let's count again.
flow.kid: Rest for two minutes. Count your breaths again.

flow.do: Breathe slowly onto a cold mirror. Look at the mist.
flow.say: Breathe on the mirror. What do you see? Where do you think that mist came from?
flow.kid: Breathe on a cold mirror. See the mist? Where did it come from?
flow.parent: After your child has guessed, explain: the mist is water from inside the body, carried out in the breath. The breath also carries out carbon dioxide, which you cannot see. If the mirror does not mist, cool it in the fridge for a few minutes first.

flow.do: 1. Multiply each middle number by 4 to get breaths in one minute. 2. Draw one bar for each.
flow.say: Fifteen seconds is a quarter of a minute. So four times the number gives breaths in a whole minute.
flow.kid: Times each middle number by 4. That gives breaths in one minute. Draw a bar for each.

check.q: In the breath counter, you breathe much faster after jumping. Why?
options: Your lungs got smaller
Your muscles need more energy, so respiration needs more oxygen
Jumping pushes extra air into your nose
check.why: Working muscles need more energy. They get it by respiration, which uses oxygen. So you breathe faster to bring in more oxygen and push out more carbon dioxide. Picking 'lungs got smaller' means guessing about size. Lungs stay the same size. Picking 'jumping pushes air in' means thinking breathing is just air being pushed, not something your body needs.

flow.do: Ask your child for three sentences: what I think, what I saw and why.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? Why?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: my body needs more air when it works hard. What I saw: I took 20 breaths a minute sitting, and 44 after jumping. Why: my muscles needed more energy, and respiration uses oxygen to get energy from food.

activities.title: The Seven Signs Trial: a seed, a cloud and a car

materials.item: a big sheet of paper and a pencil
a few dry moong seeds, and a few soaked overnight or sprouted, if you can
a toy car, or a real car you can look at in the lane
a window or a doorway where you can see the sky, or a photo of clouds on a clear day

activities.safety: Look at real cars only from the pavement, with a grown-up. Never look straight at the Sun.

schedule.what: Draw the trial table. Test a seed, a cloud and a car for each of the seven signs. Count the ticks and give a verdict.

activities.record: Fill in the trial table with a tick, a cross or a wavy line for 'sort of'. Write a verdict under each column.
activities.context: This is the seven signs trial. You test three things, a seed, a cloud and a car, against each of the seven signs of life. Then you decide which one is alive.

setup.art: A big sheet of paper with a table drawn on it: three columns headed by a seed, a cloud and a car, seven rows headed by small sign icons.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a table: three things across, seven signs down.

setup.art: A child at a window pointing at a cloud, holding a toy car in the other hand, a small steel bowl of moong seeds on the sill.
setup.caption: 2. Look at each thing. For each sign, put a tick, a cross or a wavy line.

setup.art: The finished table with ticks and crosses, and the seed column circled in green.
setup.caption: 3. Count the ticks. Give your verdict with your evidence.

flow.do: 1. Draw a table on a big sheet. 2. Across the top, draw a seed, a cloud and a car. 3. Down the side, write the seven signs: nutrition, respiration, growth, movement, sensing, excretion, reproduction.
flow.say: Today we put three things on trial. A seed, a cloud and a car. For each sign of life, we decide: does it do this? Yes, no, or sort of?
flow.kid: Draw a big table. Put a seed, a cloud and a car across the top. Write the seven signs down the side.
flow.context: This is the first step of the seven signs trial. You test a seed, a cloud and a car against the seven signs of life.

flow.do: Go through the car, one sign at a time. Mark each box with a tick, a cross or a wavy line.
flow.say: Does a car get food? It takes in petrol, so maybe a wavy line. Does it get energy from it? It burns petrol with air. Does it grow? Does it make baby cars?
flow.kid: Test the car. One sign at a time. Tick, cross, or wavy line for 'sort of'.

check.q: In the seven signs trial, a car moves, takes in petrol and gives out smoke. Is that enough to call it alive?
options: Yes, three signs is enough
No. It never grows or makes young, and people build it.
Yes, because it is fast
check.why: Living things do all seven signs over their lives. A car never grows by itself, never mends itself and never makes a baby car. People build it in a factory. Picking 'three signs is enough' is a very common idea. But a cloud and a river would then be alive too. Picking 'it is fast' means thinking movement is the main sign of life.

flow.do: Look at a cloud through the window for a few minutes. If the sky is clear today, use a photo of clouds and remember how clouds change. Then go through the seven signs for the cloud.
flow.say: Watch that cloud. Is it moving? Is it changing shape? Clouds can grow and even split into little clouds. Does a cloud eat? Does it make baby clouds of its own?
flow.kid: Watch a cloud for a few minutes. Does it move? Does it grow? Does it eat? Fill in its column.
flow.parent: A cloud moves, grows and can split. Your child may want to tick those. Ask: does it grow from the inside by using food? Or does it grow because more water vapour in the air turns into drops? A cloud never feeds, respires or makes young of its own kind. It is a heap of tiny water drops pushed by the wind.

flow.do: Look at a dry moong seed. If you have a soaked or sprouted one, look at that too. Fill in the seed column.
flow.say: A dry seed seems to do nothing. But look at this sprouted one. Is this sprout feeding? Yes, on food stored inside the seed. Is the sprout growing? Which way is the root moving?
flow.kid: Look at a dry seed. Then a sprouted one. Which signs does the seed show once they wake up? Fill in the seed's column.
flow.parent: A dry seed is dormant. Once wet, the seed feeds on stored food, respires, grows, moves the root down, senses gravity and gives out carbon dioxide. Later the plant will flower and make seeds. If you have not done the seed test yet, you can come back to this column after it.

flow.do: Count the ticks in each column. Then ask your child to give a verdict for each thing, with evidence.
flow.say: Which one did all seven? So which one is alive? Tell me your evidence like a judge.
flow.kid: Count the ticks. Which one does all seven? Give your verdict. Say what you saw. Say why.
flow.parent: A good answer: the seed is alive. Given water, the seed does all seven signs. The car and the cloud only show some signs, and they never grow from inside or make young of their own kind.
flow.think: Can you think of something that does only one or two signs of life, but is alive?

activities.title: Nature Museum Box: alive, once alive, never alive

materials.item: a bag or basket for collecting
3 shoebox lids or trays
small paper labels and a pencil
a magnifying glass

activities.safety: Go outside only with a grown-up. Do not pick up anything sharp, animal poo or dead animals. Leave living animals where they are. Draw them instead. Wash hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Collect things on a walk. Sort them into three trays. Write labels in your own words. Count each tray.

activities.record: Write a label for each thing in your own words. Count how many things are in each tray, and draw a tally.
activities.context: This is a nature walk and a museum, best if you have a park or a garden nearby. You collect things, then sort them into three trays: alive, once alive and never alive. With no park, collect around the home instead.

setup.art: A child and a parent on a park path, the child dropping a fallen leaf, a twig and a pebble into a cloth bag.
setup.caption: 1. Walk and collect small things. Leave living animals where they are.

setup.art: Three shoebox lids on a floor labelled with a sprout, a brown leaf and a grey stone, with a feather, a pebble, a flower, a seed pod and a bottle cap in them.
setup.caption: 2. Sort them into three trays: alive, once alive, never alive.

setup.art: A child writing small paper labels and placing them beside each thing, with tally marks drawn on a card.
setup.caption: 3. Write a label for each in your own words. Count each tray.

flow.do: Walk in a park, garden or lane for 10 minutes. Your child collects small things: leaves, twigs, seeds, pebbles, feathers, a flower, a bottle cap. For animals, they draw them instead. No park? Collect things at home instead. Try a vegetable peel, a pencil, a thread, a spoon and a stone from a plant pot.
flow.say: Let's collect a museum. Pick up small things that are lying on the ground. If you see an animal, don't pick them up. We'll draw them.
flow.kid: Collect small things on the ground. Leaves, twigs, seeds, stones. If you see an animal, draw them.
flow.context: This is the first step of the nature museum. You collect things on a walk, to sort into alive, once alive and never alive.

flow.do: Back home, set out three trays: alive, once alive, never alive. Your child sorts everything, one at a time, saying why.
flow.say: Pick one thing. Is it alive now? Was it once part of something alive? Or was it never alive?
flow.kid: Set out three trays. Pick one thing. Alive, once alive or never alive? Say why. Put it in a tray.
flow.parent: Fallen leaves, twigs, feathers and dry seed pods are once alive, unless the seeds inside are still alive. Ask: could these seeds still grow? A freshly picked flower is still alive for a while, then dies. Stones and bottle caps were never alive. Moss on a stone is alive, so that stone is a home for life.

check.q: In the nature museum, where does a fallen dry leaf go?
options: Alive
Once alive
Never alive
check.why: A fallen dry leaf was part of a living tree. Now it no longer feeds, grows or does any of the signs. So it is once alive. Picking 'alive' is common because leaves feel like part of nature. Picking 'never alive' means forgetting where the leaf came from.

flow.do: 1. Your child writes a label for each thing in their own words. 2. They count each tray and draw a tally.
flow.say: Write a label like a real museum. Say what it is and how you know.
