flow.kid: Write a label for each thing. Count each tray. Draw a tally mark for each one.
flow.think: Which tray has the most things? Why do you think so?

flow.do: Look closely at one once-alive thing with a magnifying glass.
flow.say: Look at this leaf up close. Can you see its veins? They once carried water through the living leaf.
flow.kid: Look at a leaf with a magnifying glass. Can you see the lines? They once carried water.

activities.title: The Shy Plant: does a plant sense touch?

materials.item: a touch-me-not plant (chhui-mui or lajwanti), in a pot or growing wild
a feather or a soft paintbrush
a clock or phone timer

activities.safety: Touch-me-not stems have small prickles. Touch the leaves gently with a feather or one fingertip, not the stem. Wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Touch one leaf and time how long it takes to open again. While you wait, compare a light touch with a firmer tap.

activities.record: Write how many minutes the leaf took to open again. Write how many pairs of leaflets folded after a light touch and after a firmer tap. Draw a leaf open, closed and opening.
activities.context: This activity is about sensing, one of the seven signs of life. You touch a touch-me-not plant and watch them respond, and time how long it takes to recover.

setup.art: A touch-me-not plant in a clay pot on a sunny step, their feathery leaves wide open.
setup.caption: 1. Find a touch-me-not plant with their leaves open.

setup.art: A feather touching the tip of one leaf, and the little leaflets folding together in pairs.
setup.caption: 2. Touch one leaf gently with a feather. Watch it fold.

setup.art: A child sitting by the plant with a phone timer showing minutes, the leaf half open again.
setup.caption: 3. Time how long it takes to open again.

flow.do: Find a touch-me-not plant with their leaves open. Do this in the daytime, in a warm place, with the plant watered. Look closely at one leaf.
flow.say: This plant is called chhui-mui, or lajwanti, or touch-me-not. Look at their little leaflets, lined up in pairs. What do you think will happen if we touch the plant?
flow.kid: This is a touch-me-not plant. Look at their tiny leaflets. What will happen if you touch the plant?
flow.context: This is the first step of the shy plant activity. You test whether a plant can sense touch.

flow.do: 1. Touch the tip of one leaf very gently with a feather. 2. Watch closely. 3. Start the timer.
flow.say: Gently now. Touch just the tip. Watch. What happens? Start the timer.
flow.kid: Touch the tip of one leaf with the feather. Watch it. Start the timer.
flow.parent: The leaflets fold together in a second or two, starting near the touch. Sometimes the fold spreads along the leaf, or the whole leaf drops. The plant does this by moving water out of special cells at the base of each leaflet. It is very fast for a plant.

check.q: When you touch a touch-me-not leaf, it folds shut. Which signs of life is the plant showing?
options: Sensing and movement
Nutrition and growth
Reproduction
check.why: The plant senses the touch and responds by moving their leaflets. That is sensing and movement. Picking 'nutrition and growth' mixes up a quick response with slow feeding and growing. Picking 'reproduction' means thinking any change is making young.

flow.do: 1. Choose a second leaf. Touch just the tip of one leaflet, as lightly as you can, with the feather. Count how many pairs fold. 2. Choose a third leaf. Tap its stalk firmly with one finger. Watch what happens.
flow.say: Let's compare. First the lightest touch you can make. How many pairs folded? Now a firm tap on another leaf. What is different?
flow.kid: Touch one leaflet very lightly. Count the pairs that fold. Then tap another leaf firmly. What is different?
flow.parent: A light touch usually folds only a few pairs near the tip. A firm tap folds the whole leaf, and the leaf stalk often droops down. The plant senses how strong the touch is, and responds more to a stronger one.

flow.do: Look at the first leaf every 5 minutes. Stop the timer when it is fully open again. Write down the minutes.
flow.say: Now we wait. Plants recover slowly. Let's check every 5 minutes. Meanwhile, why do you think the plant folds their leaves?
flow.kid: Look at the first leaf every 5 minutes. Stop the timer when it is open. Write down the minutes.
flow.parent: It often takes 10 to 30 minutes to open again. In the evening, or when it is cold, the plant folds without a touch and opens slowly, so the timing will be longer. If you cannot get a plant, watch the touch-me-not video in this unit instead. Good ideas for why: to scare off a hungry animal, to look less tasty, or to knock insects off. Scientists think it protects the plant from being eaten, but they are still testing this.

flow.do: Tell your child about J.C. Bose and the dropped plants. Then let the plant rest.
flow.say: J.C. Bose, a great Indian scientist, found that this plant folds less if you touch them again and again. In 2014, scientists dropped these plants gently many times. The plants stopped folding, and weeks later they still did not fold when dropped.
flow.kid: Scientists dropped these plants gently many times. The plants stopped folding. Weeks later, they still did not fold.
flow.think: The plants learned that the drop was safe, and remembered it. Some scientists say the plants were only tired. What do you think?

activities.title: Does a plant give out water? The bag on a branch

materials.item: 2 clear plastic bags
2 rubber bands or pieces of string
a leafy plant in a pot, on a sunny windowsill or balcony
a dry dead twig of about the same size

activities.safety: Take the bags off within a few hours so the plant does not overheat. Never put a plastic bag near anyone's face.

schedule.what: Tie one bag over a leafy branch and one over a dead twig. Leave them in the sun for 2 hours. Compare the bags.

activities.record: Draw both bags after 2 hours. Write what you see inside each.
activities.context: This activity shows that a living plant takes in water and gives out water and gases through their leaves. You tie a bag over a living branch and another over a dead twig, and compare.

setup.art: A clear plastic bag tied with a rubber band over a leafy branch of a potted hibiscus on a sunny balcony.
setup.caption: 1. Tie a clear bag over a leafy, living branch.

setup.art: A second clear bag tied over a dry dead twig stuck in a pot of soil beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Tie another bag over a dead twig. Leave both in the sun.

setup.art: Two bags side by side after two hours: the leafy one misty with water drops, the twig one clear and dry.
setup.caption: 3. After 2 hours, compare the inside of the two bags.

flow.do: 1. Water the plant. 2. Slip a clear bag over one leafy branch and tie it gently. 3. Push a dead twig into the soil and tie a bag over it. 4. Leave both in sunlight.
flow.say: We have a living branch and a dead twig. Both get a bag. If the living plant gives anything out, the bag will catch it.
flow.kid: Tie a bag over a living branch. Tie another over a dead twig. Leave them in the sun.
flow.context: This is the first step of the bag-on-a-branch activity. You find out whether a living plant gives out water.

flow.do: After 2 hours, look at both bags. Touch the outside. Then take both bags off.
flow.say: Look! What is inside the bag on the living branch? And the dead twig's bag?
flow.kid: Look at the two bags. Which one has water drops inside?

check.q: After 2 hours in the sun, the bag on the living branch is misty with water, and the bag on the dead twig is dry. Why?
options: Rain got into the first bag
The living plant took water up from their roots and gave it out through their leaves
The dead twig drank all the water
check.why: A living plant pulls water up from their roots and lets water vapour out of tiny holes in their leaves. The vapour turns back into drops on the inside of the bag. The dead twig is once alive. It no longer does this. Picking 'rain' cannot explain why only one bag is wet. Picking 'the twig drank it' means thinking a dead twig still feeds.

flow.do: Talk about what the plant takes in and gives out.
flow.say: A plant takes in water and air, and gives out water vapour and gases from their leaves. In sunlight, one gas they give out is oxygen, the gas we need.
flow.kid: A plant takes in water and air. They give out water and gases from their leaves. One gas is oxygen, which we breathe.
flow.parent: Strictly, most of this water is not waste. The plant lets it out as they pull up water and minerals from the soil, and it also cools the leaves. True plant waste includes the oxygen they make in sunlight, carbon dioxide from respiration, and waste stored in old leaves that fall.

activities.title: All Seven in Me: find the signs of life in your own body

materials.item: a 30 cm ruler
a hand mirror
a pencil and a doorframe or wall you are allowed to mark lightly

activities.safety: Drop the ruler from a low height. Do not throw it.

schedule.what: Find each sign of life in your own body. Do the ruler-catch test for sensing. Mark your height.

activities.record: Write one piece of evidence for each sign of life in your body. Write your three ruler-catch numbers.
activities.context: This activity is about finding all seven signs of life in your own body. It includes a ruler-catch test that measures how fast you sense and respond.

setup.art: A parent holding a ruler upright by its top end, and a child with finger and thumb open just below the bottom end, ready to catch.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up holds a ruler. Your fingers wait at the bottom.

setup.art: The child pinching the falling ruler, with the number at their thumb circled.
setup.caption: 2. When it drops, catch it. Read the number at your thumb.

setup.art: A child standing against a doorframe while a parent draws a small pencil line above their head, with older marks below.
setup.caption: 3. Mark your height on a doorframe. Check it again in a few months.

flow.do: Go through the signs one by one. For each, find evidence in your child's body. Nutrition: what did you eat today? Respiration and excretion: breathe on a mirror. Movement: wiggle your fingers. Growth: are your old clothes too small?
flow.say: You are a living thing. So you must do all seven signs. Let's find the evidence, one sign at a time.
flow.kid: You are alive. So you do all seven signs. Find evidence for each one in your own body.
flow.context: This is the first step of All Seven in Me. You look for each of the seven signs of life in your own body.

flow.do: Ruler catch. 1. Hold a 30 cm ruler upright by its top end, with the 0 at the bottom. 2. Your child holds finger and thumb open at the 0, not touching. 3. Without warning, let go. 4. They catch it. Read the number at their thumb. 5. Do it three times.
flow.say: This tests sensing. Your eyes see the ruler fall. Your brain sends a message. Your fingers squeeze. The smaller the number, the faster you were.
flow.kid: Get ready to catch the ruler. Don't look at the grown-up's hand. Watch the ruler. Catch it! Read the number.
flow.parent: Grown-ups usually catch it at about 15 to 25 cm. Children of this age often catch it near the end, or miss it. If they miss, write 'more than 30 cm'. That is a result too. A smaller number means a faster response. Practice can make it smaller. This is a fun way to measure sensing and responding.

flow.do: Mark your child's height lightly on a doorframe with the date.
flow.say: Growth is slow, so we need a mark. Let's check again in three months.
flow.kid: Stand against the doorframe. A grown-up marks your height. Check it again in three months.
flow.wait: Check the mark again in about three months.

flow.do: Ask your child which sign they cannot do yet.
flow.say: Which sign of life are you not doing yet? Is that all right?
flow.kid: Which sign can't you do yet? Why is that fine?

check.q: A child does six signs of life every day, but cannot make babies yet. Is the child alive?
options: No, because one sign is missing
Yes. Living things do all seven over their whole life, not every day.
Only half alive
check.why: A living thing does all seven signs over their life, not at every moment. Children grow up first, and reproduction can come much later. Picking 'no' means thinking every sign must happen all the time. A sleeping cat is not running, but is still alive.

activities.title: Who Eats What? Following food back to the Sun

materials.item: a sheet of paper and coloured pencils

schedule.what: List six living things. Find what each eats. Draw arrows from food to eater, all the way back to the Sun.

activities.record: A food chart with arrows from the Sun to plants to animals, and back to the soil.
activities.context: This activity is about nutrition, one of the seven signs of life. You draw a chart of who eats what, and find that all food starts with sunlight caught by plants.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with small drawings of a Sun, a grass patch, a cow, a spider, a crow, a mushroom and a child.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the Sun and six living things.

setup.art: The same sheet with arrows from the Sun to the grass, the grass to the cow, the cow's milk to the child, and a fallen leaf to a mushroom.
setup.caption: 2. Draw an arrow from each food to its eater.

setup.art: Extra arrows going from every animal and plant down into a brown soil strip at the bottom.
setup.caption: 3. Add arrows to the soil. What happens when living things die?

flow.do: Draw the Sun at the top, and six living things: grass, a cow, a spider, a crow, a mushroom and your child.
flow.say: Every living thing needs food. But where does the food come from in the first place? Let's follow it back.
flow.kid: Draw the Sun. Then draw grass, a cow, a spider, a crow, a mushroom and you.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Eats What. You draw a chart to find where every living thing's food comes from.

flow.do: Your child draws an arrow from each food to the thing that eats it.
flow.say: The arrow goes from the food to the eater. What does the cow eat? What does a crow eat? Where does the grass get their food?
flow.kid: Draw arrows from each food to who eats it. Where does the grass get their food?

check.q: In the food chart, where does grass get their food?
options: From the soil, by eating it
They make their own food in their leaves, using sunlight, air and water
They do not need food
check.why: Green plants make their own food, a sugar, using sunlight, air and water. They take in water and a few minerals from the soil, but the soil is not their food. Picking 'eats the soil' is a very common idea. In the 1600s, Jan Baptist van Helmont grew a willow tree in a pot for five years. The tree grew heavy, but the soil in the pot hardly lost any weight. Picking 'does not need food' forgets that all living things need nutrition.

flow.do: Add arrows from every living thing to a strip of soil at the bottom.
flow.say: When a leaf falls or an animal dies, what happens to them? Who do you think eats them?
flow.kid: Draw arrows from everything to the soil. Who eats the dead things? Mushrooms and tiny soil creatures.
flow.think: If all the food starts with sunlight, is some of the Sun inside you right now?
flow.parent: After your child has guessed, explain: mushrooms and tiny living things in the soil feed on dead leaves and animals, and turn them back into soil and air.

projects.title: Life Diary: watch a moong plant do all seven signs

materials.item: 6 moong seeds
2 small pots or paper cups with holes, filled with soil
a shoebox with a lid
scissors, for a grown-up
a ruler
a clear plastic bag and a rubber band
a notebook for the diary

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the hole in the box. Wash hands after handling soil.

schedule.what: Plant 3 seeds in each pot. Start the diary with a drawing and a guess.
Look for shoots. Measure the tallest. Which signs can you see?
A grown-up cuts a hole in one end of the shoebox. Put one pot inside, at the far end. Leave the other pot in the room.
Open the box. Compare the two pots. Measure both. Tie a bag over a few leaves of the room pot for 2 hours.
Measure again. Fill in the seven signs page. Move the strongest seedling into a bigger pot in a sunny spot, and keep watching for flowers and pods.

projects.record: A diary page for each visit: a drawing, the height of the tallest plant, and which signs of life you saw. Finish with a seven-signs page with evidence for each sign.
projects.context: In this 10-day project you grow moong plants and keep a diary. You look for evidence of each of the seven signs of life, including a shoebox test to see if plants can sense light and move towards it.

setup.art: Two paper cups of soil on a windowsill with tiny moong shoots, and a child writing in a notebook.
setup.caption: 1. Plant moong seeds in two pots. Start a life diary.

setup.art: A shoebox with a small round hole cut in one end facing a bright window, one pot inside at the far end.
setup.caption: 2. Put one pot in a shoebox with a hole at one end. Leave the other in the room.

setup.art: The box opened: its seedlings bent sharply towards the hole, long and pale, next to the room pot's straighter green seedlings.
setup.caption: 3. After 3 days, open the box and compare. Which way did the shoots grow?

flow.do: 1. Fill two pots with soil. 2. Push 3 moong seeds into each, about 1 cm deep. 3. Water gently. 4. Start the diary: draw the pots and write a guess.
flow.say: We will keep a life diary for 10 days. Our job is to catch the moong plant doing every sign of life.
flow.kid: Plant 3 seeds in each pot. Water them. Start your diary. Draw the pots.
flow.context: This is the first step of the life diary project. You grow moong plants and look for all seven signs of life.

flow.do: On day 3, look for shoots. Measure the tallest one. Write which signs you can see.
flow.say: Look, shoots! Which signs of life can you see already?
flow.kid: Look for shoots. Measure the tallest one. Which signs can you see? Write them down.

flow.do: On day 4, a grown-up cuts a hole about 3 cm wide in one short end of the shoebox. Put one pot inside, at the far end. Put the lid on. Point the hole at a bright window. Leave the other pot in the room. Water both the same, opening the box quickly.
flow.say: Plants can't walk. But can they move towards light? This box will tell us.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts a hole in the box. Put one pot inside. Point the hole at the window. Leave the other pot out.

flow.do: On day 7, open the box. Compare the two pots. Measure both. Then tie a clear bag over a few leaves of the room pot for 2 hours.
flow.say: Look at the box plants. Which way did they grow? How did they know where the light was?
flow.kid: Open the box. Which way did the shoots grow? Measure both pots. Tie a bag over some leaves.

check.q: In the life diary, the moong shoots in the shoebox bent towards the hole. Which signs of life does that show?
options: Sensing and movement
Reproduction
Excretion only
check.why: The shoot tips sensed which side the light came from. Then the shaded side grew faster, so the shoots bent towards the light. That is sensing and movement, done by growing. Picking 'reproduction' means thinking any change is making young. Picking 'excretion' mixes up bending with getting rid of waste.

flow.parent: The box seedlings may be long and pale. They used their stored food to stretch towards the light. A substance in the shoot, called auxin, gathers on the shaded side and makes those cells grow longer.

flow.do: On day 10, measure again. Make a seven-signs page: one line of evidence for each sign. Then move the strongest seedling into a bigger pot on a sunny windowsill or balcony.
flow.say: Let's check our diary. Did we catch every sign of life? Which one haven't we seen yet?
flow.kid: Measure your plants. Write one piece of evidence for each sign. Which sign is still missing?
flow.parent: Reproduction will be missing. A moong plant takes about a month or more to flower and grow pods with seeds. They need at least four to six hours of direct sun a day. Keep watching the plant. When it makes pods, open one. New seeds! That is the seventh sign. On a shady balcony the plant may not flower. Then look at the moong in your kitchen: every one of those seeds grew in a pod on a moong plant.
flow.think: When your plant makes new seeds, will they be alive too? What will they need to wake up?

challenges.title: Design a Life Detector for Mars
challenges.problem: A robot on Mars will scoop up some soil. Your job is to design tests that could tell whether anything in the soil is alive. Test your design on three mystery cups at home.
constraints: You cannot see anything alive, even with a magnifying glass.
You can only use tests based on the seven signs of life.

A grown-up secretly prepares three mystery cups, each with 2 tablespoons of atta. A has half a teaspoon of dry yeast mixed in. B is plain atta. C has half a teaspoon of baking soda mixed in. Mix well, so the cups look the same.
materials: 3 small cups with 2 tablespoons of atta in each, prepared by a grown-up and labelled A, B and C
half a cup of warm sugar water, with the juice of half a lemon stirred in
a little boiling water, for a grown-up only
general: Give each sample food and warmth, then watch for signs of life, like gas bubbles. A living thing should feed and give out waste.
Watch for a long time, not just a moment. Living things keep going and often speed up as they grow. A chemical fizz starts at once and soon stops.
Run a control. A grown-up heats one spoon of each sample with boiling water first. Heat kills living things. If the bubbles stop after heating, something alive was probably making them.
creative: In 1976, the Viking robots on Mars really did a test like this. They fed the soil and watched for gas. Gas came out, and heating the soil stopped it. Gilbert Levin, who designed the test, thought it found life. Most scientists think strange chemicals in Martian soil made the gas. They still argue about it.
Could you test for growth? Check if the bubbles get faster over an hour.
Could you test for sensing? Living things might respond differently in the cold, in the dark or with no food.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own life detector. Draw it, list its tests, and say what result would make you shout 'Life!'. What result would trick you?
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You design tests that could find life in soil from Mars, and try them on three mystery cups of atta.

setup.art: Three small cups of atta labelled A, B and C on a tray, with a cup of sugar water and a spoon beside them.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up prepares three mystery cups of atta. You do not know which is which.

setup.art: A child stirring sugar water into each cup of atta: cup C fizzing at once, cups A and B still.
setup.caption: 2. Stir warm sugar water into each cup. Watch at once, then every 10 minutes.

setup.art: Thirty minutes later: cup A puffed up and full of bubbles, cup C now flat and still, cup B unchanged.
setup.caption: 3. After 30 minutes, which cup is still bubbling and growing?

flow.do: Talk about the problem. Ask your child which signs of life a robot could test from far away.
flow.say: We can't send a scientist to Mars. A robot has to do the tests. Which signs of life could a robot check?
flow.kid: A robot on Mars scoops up soil. How could it tell if anything in the soil is alive? Which signs could it test?

ask.q: Which signs could a robot test?
good: Give it food and see if it eats.
See if it gives out gas.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Mars life detector challenge. You design tests to find life you cannot see.

flow.do: 1. Stir 3 tablespoons of warm sugar water with lemon into each mystery cup, to make a thick batter. 2. Watch straight away. 3. Then look every 10 minutes for 30 minutes. 4. Write what you see in each cup each time.
flow.say: Watch closely. Something might happen fast, or slowly. Write it all down.
flow.kid: Stir sugar water into each cup. Watch at once. Then look every 10 minutes. Write what you see.
flow.parent: Cup C fizzes at once, because baking soda reacts with lemon juice. It stops within a minute or two. Cup A starts slowly. After 10 to 20 minutes, small bubbles appear, and the batter keeps getting puffier. Cup B does nothing much. This shows how a non-living chemical reaction can trick a life detector.

flow.do: A grown-up stirs a spoon of dry powder from A and from C into a little boiling water. Let them cool for 5 minutes, until just warm. Then stir in sugar water with lemon and watch.
flow.say: This is our control. Heat kills living things, but chemicals don't care. If the bubbles stop after heating, they were made by something alive.
flow.kid: A grown-up mixes some of A and C with boiling water. Wait until it cools. Add sugar water. Do they still bubble?

check.q: In the Mars life detector test, cup A bubbled slowly and kept going, but stopped bubbling after it was heated. Cup C fizzed at once, even after heating. Which cup had something alive?
options: Cup C, because it fizzed most
Cup A, because its bubbles grew slowly and heating stopped them
Neither, because bubbles are never a sign of life
check.why: The yeast in cup A fed on sugar, respired and gave out gas, slowly and steadily. Heat killed the yeast, so the bubbles stopped. Baking soda in cup C is not alive. It fizzes with lemon juice, heated or not. Picking 'cup C' means thinking more bubbles means more life. Picking 'neither' is close, because one sign alone is not proof. But together, slow growing bubbles that stop when heated are good evidence.

flow.do: Your child draws their own life detector and lists its tests.
flow.say: Now invent your own detector. What tests would you add? What result would make you sure? What could trick you?
flow.kid: Draw your own life detector. List its tests. What would make you shout 'Life!'?

challenges.title: A World in a Jar: keep life going with the lid shut
challenges.problem: Build a closed jar that keeps a small plant alive for at least two weeks, with the lid shut from the first day. You may not add food or water once it is closed.
constraints: Once the lid is on, you cannot open it for two weeks.
You can only use things from home, or from a plant nursery.
The jar must stay where it gets light, but not hot direct sun.
materials: a big clear glass jar with a lid, like an old pickle jar
small stones from a plant pot, or broken bits of an old clay pot
soil from a plant pot, or potting soil from a nursery
a small plant, like a money plant cutting with roots, or a small fern
a spoon and a little water
general: Put small stones at the bottom so extra water can drain out of the soil.
Add soil, then the plant. Water just enough to make the soil damp, not wet.
Close the lid and keep the jar near a bright window, out of hot sun.
creative: In 1960, a man in England, David Latimer, planted a bottle garden. He last watered it in 1972 and kept it sealed for decades. It was still growing, using light, its own water and its own air.
If you have a garden, add a pinch of damp leaf litter with its tiny soil creatures, to break down dead leaves. Could the jar recycle its own waste?
Make two jars: one in light, one in a dark cupboard. Which plant keeps doing the signs of life?
challenges.your_turn: Design your own jar world. Draw it with labels. After two weeks, say which signs of life you saw inside, and where the water and air went.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You build a closed jar garden that keeps a plant alive with no new food or water, using only light from outside.

setup.art: A big glass pickle jar with a layer of small stones at the bottom and a layer of dark soil above.
setup.caption: 1. Put small stones in the bottom of a big jar, then soil.

setup.art: Small hands placing a money plant cutting into the soil, with a spoon dripping water.
setup.caption: 2. Plant a small plant. Add a little water. Close the lid.

setup.art: The closed jar on a bright windowsill, water droplets on the inside of the glass and a fresh green leaf on the plant.
setup.caption: 3. Keep it in the light. Watch for drops and new leaves for two weeks.

flow.do: 1. Wash the jar. 2. Put 2 cm of stones in the bottom. 3. Add 5 cm of damp soil. 4. Plant the cutting. 5. Add 2 spoons of water. 6. Close the lid.
flow.say: We're making a tiny world. Once the lid is on, nothing goes in and nothing comes out, except light. Can life keep going?
flow.kid: Stones first. Then soil. Then your plant. Two spoons of water. Close the lid.
flow.context: This is the first step of the jar world challenge. You build a closed jar where a plant must keep themselves alive.

flow.do: Put the jar near a bright window, out of hot direct sun. Look at it every day for a few seconds.
flow.say: Each day, look for drops on the glass, new leaves, and anything that changes.
flow.kid: Put the jar near a window. Look every day. Do you see drops on the glass? New leaves?
flow.wait: Look once a day for 2 weeks.

flow.do: After 2 weeks, look closely. Your child lists every sign of life they saw.
flow.say: The plant had no new water and no new air for two weeks. How did they keep going?
flow.kid: After two weeks, look closely. Which signs of life did you see?

check.q: A plant stayed alive in a closed jar for two weeks with no new water. Where did their water come from?
options: The water went round and round: from soil to plant to air to glass and back to soil
The plant made new water from light
The plant did not need any water
check.why: The plant took water from the soil and let it out from their leaves. The water turned into drops on the glass and ran back down into the soil. The same water was used again and again. The plant also used light to make food, and the gases they gave out were used again. Picking 'made water from light' means thinking light is a kind of water. Picking 'did not need water' forgets that all living things need water.

flow.do: Your child draws the jar with arrows for water, air and light.
flow.say: Draw your jar world. Show where the water goes, and where the light comes from.
flow.kid: Draw your jar. Draw arrows for the water going round. Draw the light coming in.
flow.think: Is the Earth a bit like a jar world? What comes in from outside, and what goes round and round?

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 3, spotted signs of life at home today. Match each sign to what she saw.
pairs: Her goldfish ate the flakes she dropped in
Her body got energy from her breakfast idli, using oxygen
She breathed out carbon dioxide and passed wee
The crow at the window flew off when she clapped
Her school shoes from last year are now too small
The money plant's leaves turned towards the window
The neighbour's cat had three kittens
items.a: see pairs
items.why: Each sign of life is one job that living things do. Spotting them in everyday life shows you know what each word means.

items.p: Getting energy out of food, inside every cell of the body, is called ____.
items.why: Respiration happens in every cell, all day and all night. Most living things use oxygen for it.

items.p: Many people think breathing and respiration mean the same thing. Which sentence is right?
opts: They are two words for the same thing
Respiration happens only inside the lungs
Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs. Respiration happens in every cell and gets energy from food
items.why: Breathing brings in the oxygen that respiration uses. Respiration itself happens in every cell, even in plants, which have no lungs. A strong answer keeps the two words apart.

items.p: An auto rickshaw moves, takes in fuel and gives out smoke. Which sign of life does the auto NOT show?
opts: Growing from inside and making young autos
items.why: An auto shows a few signs, but people build it and repair it. It never grows from inside and never makes a baby auto. So a few signs are not enough to be alive.

items.p: A tulsi plant on the balcony shows movement, even though the plant never walks anywhere.
items.why: True. Plants move by growing. Their leaves turn to the light and their roots grow down. A touch-me-not plant can even fold their leaves in a second.

items.p: Sort these into Alive, Once alive and Never alive.
items.a: see items
items.why: Alive things do the signs of life now. Once-alive things were part of a living thing, like a shell from a coconut palm, cotton from a cotton plant or wool from a sheep. Never-alive things were never part of a living thing.

items.p: In the seed test, cup C had boiled seeds on wet cotton. What did cup C help you find out?
opts: That boiling makes seeds grow faster
That water alone does not make a seed grow. The seed must be alive too
That seeds do not need water
items.why: The boiled seeds got the same water as the soaked seeds, but never grew. So water was not the difference. Life was. A strong answer says what cup C was compared with: cup A.

items.p: In the balloon test, bottle B had yeast and warm water, but no sugar. Before you try it, predict what bottle B's balloon will do.
opts: Grow the most of all three
Grow only a little, because the yeast have almost no food
items.why: Yeast are alive and need food to give out gas. Sugar is their food. Without sugar, they make very little gas. Picking 'grow the most' forgets that living things need food.

items.p: A child grows taller because her body builds new cells out of the food she eats.
items.why: True. Living things grow from inside. Cells use food to build new cells, so the body gets bigger. A cloud or a crystal only gets bigger when more stuff is added to the outside.

items.p: Breathing out carbon dioxide, sweating and passing wee all get rid of waste from inside the body. This sign of life is called ____.
items.why: Excretion is getting rid of waste that the body made. Plants excrete too, through tiny holes in their leaves.

items.p: A dry neem leaf lies on the ground. Which is the best evidence that the leaf is no longer alive?
opts: The leaf no longer takes in water or grows, and will never make anything new
The leaf is on the ground
items.why: Colour, place and weight do not tell you about life. What matters is what the leaf does. A dead leaf does none of the signs of life, so the leaf is once alive.

items.p: Ananya, a girl in Class 4, wants to explain to her little brother Ravi why a cloud is not alive, even though a cloud moves and grows. Write what she could say.
items.a: Ananya could say: 'A cloud moves because the wind pushes it. A cloud grows because more water vapour in the air cools into drops. It does not eat, respire or make baby clouds of its own. Living things do all seven signs, not just one or two.'
items.why: A strong answer explains why the cloud moves and grows, then names signs the cloud does not show.

items.p: Look at your seed test table. Which cup shows most clearly that a dry seed is alive? Write the cup, what happened in it, and why that shows the seed is alive.
items.a: Cup B. The dry seeds did nothing for five days. When I put them on wet cotton, they swelled and sprouted within a day or two. Boiled seeds never sprout, so the dry seeds must have been alive all along.
items.why: A strong answer names one cup, gives a real result from the table, and compares it with the boiled seeds or the beads.

items.p: Draw yourself doing three of the seven signs of life. Label each sign.
items.a: For example: eating a dosa, labelled nutrition. Jumping, labelled movement. Pulling a hand away from a hot tawa, labelled sensing.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a real action for each sign and uses the right word for it.

items.p: A moong seed grows into a plant that makes new seeds. Put these in order, from first to last.
items: a seed that has soaked up water
a seed with a root poking out
a plant with pods full of new seeds
items.why: The seed wakes, grows a root, then a shoot and leaves. Later the plant flowers and makes pods with new seeds. Then the circle starts again.

items.p: Meera, a girl in Class 3, asks her family: 'Is curd alive?'

views.says: Curd is alive. A spoon of yesterday's curd turns warm milk into new curd overnight.
Curd is not alive. Most of a bowl of curd is milk that has changed, and milk is not alive. It is food, like rice.
Curd is not one living thing. It is full of tiny living things called bacteria. They are what is alive.

items.ask: Who do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses a sign of life. For Amma: the bacteria in curd make more of themselves in warm milk, which is reproduction. For Paati: the living part is the bacteria, not the whole bowl. For Farhan: most of the curd really is changed milk. Answering back, a strong answer says what is true in another view.
items.why: Each person sees something true. A strong answer gives evidence, like setting curd from milk, and is fair to another side.

items.p: A tulsi plant sits in a closed jar world, in the dark, for one whole night. What is the plant doing?
opts: Nothing at all until the morning
Respiring: using sugar and oxygen for energy, and giving out carbon dioxide
items.why: Plants respire all the time, day and night, like animals. In the dark they cannot make food, so they only respire. A strong answer names respiration and the gas given out.

items.p: Which of these is NOT true excretion, because it is mostly food the body could not use?
items.why: Poo is mostly water, gut bacteria and food that was never digested. Scientists call it egestion. Wee, sweat and carbon dioxide are waste made inside the body. A strong answer says where each waste comes from.

items.p: Sneha, a girl in Class 4, counted 11 breaths in 15 seconds, just after skipping. How many breaths is that in one minute?
items.why: One minute is four lots of 15 seconds. So 11 times 4 is 44. Picking 11 forgets to multiply. Picking 60 mixes up seconds with breaths.

items.p: After jumping, most children breathe about twice as fast as when they sit still. Why?
opts: Jumping squeezes the air out of their lungs
The air gets thinner when they move
Their muscles need more energy, so their cells respire faster and need more oxygen
items.why: Respiration gives muscles their energy, and it uses oxygen. Working muscles need more energy, so the body takes in air faster. The breath counter shows this in numbers.

items.p: Sort these. Can only living things do this, or can non-living things do it too?
cats: Non-living things can do this too
items: Non-living things can do this too
Non-living things can do this too
Non-living things can do this too
making young of their own kind
Non-living things can do this too
items.a: see items
items.why: A cloud gets bigger, a car uses energy and a river moves. But only living things grow from inside, respire, are made of cells and make young of their own kind. That is why one sign is never enough.

items.p: Every living thing makes young of their own kind, but in different ways. Match each one to how they make young.
pairs: kids born alive from the mother
small buds that grow and break off
tiny spores carried by the air
items.a: see pairs
items.why: There are many ways to make young, but the young are always the same kind of living thing as the parent.

items.p: A mule almost never has young. Even so, a mule is fully alive.
items.why: True. A mule's body feeds, respires, grows, moves, senses and gets rid of waste. Making young is a sign for a kind of living thing, not for every single one.

items.p: In the bag-on-a-branch activity, drops of ____ formed inside the bag on the living branch, but not inside the bag on the dead twig.
items.why: The living plant pulled water up from the soil and let it out through tiny holes in the leaves. The dead twig did nothing. A strong answer can say what the dead twig was compared with.

items.p: Revathi, a girl in Class 5, sets up the balloon test. Bottle A gets warm water and one spoon of yeast. Bottle C gets cold water and three spoons of yeast. Why can't she tell whether the cold made bottle C slow? What should she change?
items.a: She changed two things at once: the water and the amount of yeast. So she cannot tell which one made the difference. She should put the same amount of yeast and sugar in both, and change only the water.
items.why: A strong answer names both changes and says a fair test changes only one thing.

items.p: In the shoebox test, the moong shoots bent towards the hole. Which two signs of life does this show? Explain how you know.
items.a: Sensing and movement. The shoots sensed where the light came from. Then they moved by growing, bending towards the hole. The shoots in the open room grew straight up.
items.why: A strong answer names both signs and links each to what the shoots did, ideally comparing them with the pot outside the box.

items.p: Follow the energy in your breakfast idli back to the Sun. Write each step in order.
items.a: The Sun shone on rice and urad dal plants. The plants used sunlight to make sugar and starch, and stored this food in their grains. The grains were ground into batter and steamed into idli. I ate the idli, and my cells respire to get the energy out.
items.why: A strong answer has every step, from sunlight to the plant's stored food to your cells, with no gap.

items.p: In 2014, scientists dropped touch-me-not plants a short, harmless distance again and again. After a while, the plants stopped folding their leaves when dropped. Weeks later, they still did not fold when dropped. But they did fold when shaken in a new way.

views.who: Monica Gagliano, a scientist in Australia who ran the test
views.says: The plants learned that the drop was harmless, and remembered it for weeks.
Learning and memory are words for animals with brains. We need more tests before we use them for plants.

views.who: J.C. Bose, a scientist in Kolkata, about 100 years ago
views.says: Plants respond to the world much as animals do. Their signals are like the signals in our nerves.

items.ask: Did the plants learn? Pick the view you agree with most and give your evidence. Then say what one of the others has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses the evidence. The plants still folded when shaken in a new way, so they were not just tired. That supports Gagliano. Answering back, it admits that one test is not enough, and that scientists still argue about the words.
items.why: This is a real argument among scientists. There is no single right answer. A strong answer uses the shaking result.

items.p: Draw the four cups of the seed test as they looked on day 6. Under each cup, write one word: alive, dead or never alive.
items.a: Cup A: sprouted seeds, 'alive'. Cup B: seeds just starting to sprout after their water, 'alive'. Cup C: boiled seeds, unchanged, 'dead'. Cup D: beads, unchanged, 'never alive'.
items.why: A strong drawing tells cups B, C and D apart. Cup B is alive even though the seeds started late.

items.p: A crow's feather has fallen onto the balcony. Which of these is true?
opts: The feather comes alive when wet
The feather is once alive. The feather was part of a living crow, but no longer grows
items.why: A feather grew on a living bird, so the feather is once alive. On the balcony, the feather does none of the signs of life. The crow, flying off somewhere, is still alive.

items.p: A flower picked from a plant is still alive for a while.
items.why: True. A freshly picked flower still takes in water and respires for a few days. Then the flower slowly dies, because they can no longer get food and water from the plant.

items.p: Kavya turns a sprouting moong seed upside down, so the root points up. Predict what the root will do over the next day.
opts: Bend round and grow downwards again
items.why: Roots sense gravity and grow down, wherever the seed is facing. This is sensing and movement at the same time.

items.p: Where is the line between living and non-living? Three views.

views.who: J.C. Bose, a scientist in Kolkata, in 1902
views.says: A metal wire and a plant both tire when tapped, and both recover with rest. The line between living and non-living is not as sharp as we think.
There is a clear line. Living things are made of cells, feed, grow from inside and make young. A wire does none of these.
There are living beings in earth, water, fire and air, each with one sense, touch.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Use evidence from this unit. Then say what one of the other views gets right.
items.a: A strong answer uses the seven signs as evidence and is fair. For the biologists: a wire never feeds or grows. For Bose: the wire and the plant really did tire in the same way. For the Jain view: it reminds us that where we draw the line is partly a choice.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A strong answer weighs at least two views with evidence.

items.p: Your body keeps replacing many of its cells. Your red blood cells last only about four months. Lakshmi, aged 10, her brother Vikram, aged 8, and their grandmother talk about it.

views.says: I am the same person as last year. I have the same name, the same memories and the same face.
I am not the same. Many of my cells are new, so I am made of different stuff now.
You are like the Kaveri river. The water in it keeps changing, but the river stays the Kaveri.

items.ask: Who do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then say what another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses a fact from the unit, like cells being replaced or atoms coming from food, and is fair to another side. Many people end up close to the grandmother: the stuff changes, the pattern stays.
items.why: This is an old question with no single right answer. A strong answer gives a reason, not just a feeling.

items.p: Predict: what happens to a moong seedling kept in total darkness for three weeks, with water but no light?
opts: They turn back into a seed
They grow tall and pale, use up their stored food, and then die
They make food from water alone
items.why: A seedling lives on the food stored in the seed at first. After that, they need light to make food. In the dark, the store runs out. All the energy in a plant's food comes from the Sun.

items.p: In the 1860s, Louis Pasteur, a French scientist, boiled soup in a flask with a long, bent neck. Dust from the air got stuck in the bend. The soup stayed clear for months. When he broke the neck off, the soup went cloudy with tiny living things. What did this show?
opts: The tiny living things came in on dust from the air. They did not grow out of the soup
Soup turns into living things by itself
items.why: The soup only went cloudy when dust could fall in. So living things come only from other living things. A strong answer explains why the bent neck mattered.

items.p: All living things on Earth, from bacteria to banyan trees to you, use the same kind of instructions, called DNA. What do most scientists think this shows?
opts: People put DNA into living things
All life on Earth is related, from one shared ancestor long ago
All living things are the same size
items.why: Sharing one code is strong evidence that all living things are one big family. Plants, fungi and bacteria have DNA too.

items.p: A single bacterium, made of just one cell, feeds, respires, gets rid of waste and makes more of themselves, all on their own.
items.why: True. One cell can be a whole living being. The bacteria in curd each do all the life processes, and they make more of themselves by splitting in two.

items.p: In the life detector challenge, a grown-up made three mystery cups of atta. Sort each result: does it point to something living, or could ordinary chemistry do it?
items: fizzes at once, then stops within two minutes
starts slowly, then keeps getting puffier for 30 minutes
still fizzes after the powder was boiled and cooled
stops bubbling after the powder was boiled and cooled
items.a: see items
items.why: Living things start slowly and keep going, because they feed and multiply. Boiling kills them. A chemical reaction is fast, stops when used up, and still works after boiling.

items.p: In the life detector challenge, the baking soda cup fizzed as soon as the sugar water with lemon went in. Why could that cup trick a robot life detector? Which extra test caught the trick?
items.a: Baking soda and lemon juice make gas by a chemical reaction, with nothing alive in them. A detector that only looks for gas would think it found life. The trick was caught by boiling the powder first: the baking soda still fizzed, but the yeast cup stopped.
items.why: A strong answer explains the reaction is not life, and names the boiling test as the control.

items.p: Moss on a dry wall looks brown and dead in April. After the first rain, the moss turns green again. Is the dry moss alive? Use the seed test to back up your answer.
items.a: The dry moss is alive, but resting, like the dry seeds in cup B. The dry seeds did nothing until they got water, then they sprouted. Boiled seeds never did. The moss also wakes up with water, so the moss was dormant, not dead.
items.why: A strong answer compares the moss with the dry seeds and says why 'dead' cannot be right: dead things never wake.

items.p: Nandini, a girl in Class 5, says: 'Plants get their food from the soil. That is why they need soil.' What is the mistake?
opts: Plants make their own food from air, water and sunlight. Soil gives them water and minerals, not food energy
Plants eat insects from the soil
Plants do not need any food
items.why: This is one of the most common ideas, even among grown-ups. In the 1600s, Jan Baptist van Helmont grew a willow tree in a pot for five years. The tree gained a lot of weight, but the soil lost almost none.

items.p: Scientists have made a whole living cell from scratch, starting only with non-living chemicals.
items.why: False. Scientists have built a full set of DNA and put it into a bacterium, where it worked. But nobody has yet built a whole living cell from non-living chemicals.

items.p: What would happen to the animals in a forest if the Sun stopped shining for a whole year?
opts: Nothing, because animals do not need the Sun
Only the plants would be affected
The plants could not make food, so plant-eaters and then meat-eaters would starve
The animals would eat soil instead
items.why: Almost all the energy in food starts as sunlight caught by plants. Every food chain in the forest leads back to the plants, and the plants lead back to the Sun.

items.p: Follow one carbon atom on a journey. Put the steps in order.
items: The atom is in the air, as part of carbon dioxide
A rice plant's leaf takes the carbon dioxide in
The atom becomes part of a grain of rice
You eat the rice, and the atom becomes part of you
You breathe the atom out again, as part of carbon dioxide
items.why: The same atoms move between air, plants and animals, again and again. Living and non-living things share the same atoms.

items.p: Draw your jar world with the lid shut. Use blue arrows for water and red arrows for the gases the plant takes in and gives out.
items.a: Blue arrows from the soil up into the plant, out of the leaves, onto the glass as drops, and down into the soil. Red arrows: the plant takes in carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen in the light, and takes in oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide all the time.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that nothing leaves the jar. Water and gases go round and round.

items.p: Make your own definition of life in one sentence. Then test it on a cloud, a dry seed and a mule. Does your definition put each one in the right place? If not, fix it.
items.a: For example: 'A living thing feeds, grows and makes young.' The cloud is out, which is right. But the mule never has young, and the dry seed does not feed for now. So I change it to: 'A living thing is made of cells and, at some time in their life, feeds, grows and comes from parents.'
items.why: A strong answer tests the definition honestly, finds where it fails, and improves it. Scientists do exactly this.

items.p: In 1897, Eduard Buchner, a German scientist, crushed yeast and squeezed out the juice. The juice had no living cells, but it still turned sugar into gas. What did this show?
opts: The chemistry inside living cells can work outside them too. There is no special 'life force' in the chemicals
items.why: Before this, many scientists thought only a living cell, with a special life force, could do this chemistry. Buchner showed the chemicals could do it alone. What is special about life is how it all works together.

quiz.p: A dog hears her name, pricks up her ears and runs to the door. Which two signs of life is she showing?
quiz.why: Hearing her name is sensing. Running to the door is movement. Respiration is going on too, inside her cells, but you cannot see it here.

quiz.p: A hen's eggs hatch into chicks. Which sign of life is this?
quiz.why: Reproduction is making young of your own kind. The chicks will grow up into hens and roosters.

quiz.p: Tanvi, a girl in Class 3, is filling in a seven-signs table for a steel spoon. How many signs of life should she tick?
quiz.why: A spoon does not feed, respire, grow, move by itself, sense, excrete or make young. Steel was never part of a living thing.

quiz.p: A ceiling fan moves round and round very fast. Why is moving not enough to show that the fan is alive?
opts: Non-living things can move too. A living thing shows all the signs together
Moving is not a sign of life
quiz.why: Moving is a sign of life, but clouds, rivers and fans move too. One sign alone is never enough.

quiz.p: If a thing grows bigger, that proves it is alive.
quiz.why: False. A cloud grows bigger, and so does a salt crystal. Living things grow from inside, using food. One sign is not enough.

quiz.p: Bhavana, a girl in Class 4, tests yeast in two bottles of warm water. She adds sugar to one bottle and not to the other. What is she testing?
opts: Whether yeast need sugar, their food, to make gas
quiz.why: She changed only one thing, the sugar. So any difference in the balloons must come from the sugar. That makes it a fair test.

quiz.p: In the seed test, every cup got the same amount of water and sat in the same warm place. Why?
opts: So that the cups look neat
So that the only difference between the cups was what was in them: soaked, dry or boiled seeds, or beads
Because seeds only grow in a row
So the cotton does not dry out
quiz.why: A fair test keeps everything the same except the one thing you are testing. Then any difference must come from that one thing.

quiz.p: On a sunny day, which gas does a green plant give out more of than they take in?
quiz.why: In sunlight, plants make food and give out oxygen. They also respire and use some oxygen, but they make more than they use.

quiz.p: A touch-me-not plant senses a touch and folds their leaflets within a second or two.
quiz.why: True. This shows two signs of life at once: sensing and movement.
Wood comes from a tree that was alive. The bat does no signs of life now, so the bat is once alive.
Clay comes from the earth. It was never part of a living thing. A plant growing in the pot is alive, but the pot is not.

quiz.p: Where did the energy in a glass of milk come from, in the end?
quiz.why: The cow ate grass. The grass caught sunlight and stored its energy as food. So the energy in milk began as sunlight.

quiz.p: Which of these questions do scientists still not know the answer to?
opts: How the very first living thing on Earth began
quiz.why: There are ideas, like warm ponds or hot springs deep in the sea, but nobody knows yet. The other questions have been answered by tests.

applications: Doctors check signs of life, like breathing, a heartbeat and the eyes responding to light, to see if someone needs help.
First-aid training teaches you to check if a person is breathing, which is a sign that respiration is going on.
Farmers test seeds before sowing. They put 100 seeds on wet paper and count how many sprout.
Bakers use living yeast to make bread rise, and cooks rely on tiny living things to ferment idli and dosa batter.
Fridges, salting, drying and pickling keep food fresh by slowing down the tiny living things that spoil it.
Seed banks store dry, dormant seeds for many years. India's National Genebank in New Delhi keeps hundreds of thousands of seed samples.
Space scientists design life detectors for robots on Mars and for future missions to icy moons.
Compost pits use living worms, fungi and bacteria to turn kitchen waste back into soil.
Water testers check drinking water for living bacteria that could make people ill.
Gardeners grow new plants from cuttings, like a money plant in a bottle of water.
Scientists measure plants' electrical signals, as J.C. Bose did, to learn how plants sense damage and dryness.
Engineers build soft robots that copy how plants grow and how touch-me-not leaves fold.

open_questions.q: How did the very first living thing come from non-living chemicals?
open_questions.why_open: It happened about 4,000 million years ago and left no clear traces. Scientists test ideas in labs, but nobody has made life from plain chemicals yet.

open_questions.q: Is there life anywhere else in the universe?
open_questions.why_open: We have only ever found life on Earth. Scientists are searching on Mars and planning missions to icy moons like Europa and Enceladus, which have hidden oceans.

open_questions.q: Is there a sharp line between living and non-living, or a gentle slope?
open_questions.why_open: Most things are easy to sort, but some, like viruses and dormant seeds, are not. Scientists do not agree on one definition of life.

open_questions.q: What is it like for a plant to feel a touch?
open_questions.why_open: Plants feel. Scientists can measure the electrical signal a touch sets off inside a plant. But nobody knows how to measure what the touch is like for the plant.

open_questions.q: How does a plant remember, with no brain?
open_questions.why_open: Plants remember: the dropped touch-me-not plants seemed to remember for weeks that the drop was safe. Scientists are still finding out where in a plant such a memory could be kept. Some say 'memory' is the wrong word, and more tests are under way.

open_questions.q: Could people one day build a living cell from scratch?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have built a full set of instructions, DNA, and put it into a bacterium, where it worked. But building a whole living cell from non-living parts has not been done.

open_questions.q: Why does all life on Earth use the same code?
open_questions.why_open: It points to one shared ancestor. But why this code, and not another, is still not understood.

maths.problem: In the balloon test, all three flat balloons measured 12 cm round at the start. After 30 minutes, balloon A measured 30 cm round, and balloon B, with no sugar, measured 14 cm. How much did each balloon grow? How much more did balloon A grow than balloon B?
maths.answer: Balloon A grew 18 cm and balloon B grew 2 cm. Balloon A grew 16 cm more.
maths.explain: Balloon A: 30 take away 12 is 18 cm. Balloon B: 14 take away 12 is 2 cm. Then 18 take away 2 is 16. So balloon A grew 16 cm more than balloon B. Measuring the growth, not just the end size, shows how little the unfed yeast did.
maths.context: This is about the balloon test. You put yeast in bottles with different mixtures and stretched a balloon over each. The more gas the living yeast made, the bigger the balloon grew.

chart.title: Distance round each balloon after 30 minutes (each started at 12 cm)

maths.why_maths: Both balloons started at 12 cm, so only the growth tells us how much gas the yeast made. Taking away the starting size shows the real difference.

maths.problem: In the breath counter, a child counted 6 breaths in 15 seconds sitting still, and 11 breaths in 15 seconds just after jumping. How many breaths is each in one minute?
maths.answer: 24 breaths a minute sitting still, and 44 breaths a minute after jumping.
maths.explain: There are four lots of 15 seconds in one minute. So multiply each count by 4. 6 times 4 is 24. 11 times 4 is 44. After jumping, the child breathed 20 more times a minute.
maths.context: This is about the breath counter. You counted your breaths for 15 seconds sitting still, and again after jumping for one minute.
maths.why_maths: Counting for a whole minute is hard to do accurately. Counting for 15 seconds and multiplying by 4 is quicker, and doctors and nurses do exactly this.

maths.problem: In the seed test, 4 of the 5 soaked seeds in cup A sprouted. What fraction of the seeds sprouted? What fraction did not?
maths.answer: Four fifths sprouted. One fifth did not.
maths.explain: There were 5 seeds, so each seed is one fifth of the cup. 4 seeds sprouted, so four fifths sprouted. 1 seed did not, so one fifth did not. Four fifths and one fifth make five fifths, the whole cup.
maths.context: This is about the seed test. You put 5 moong seeds in each of four cups, some wet, some dry and some boiled, and counted how many sprouted.

chart.title: Cup A: soaked seeds on wet cotton

maths.why_maths: Seed packets and farmers say how many seeds out of every hundred will grow. A fraction tells us how alive a batch of seeds is.

maths.problem: In the ruler-catch test, a child caught the ruler at 18 cm, then 12 cm, then 15 cm. Put the three catches in order from fastest to slowest. Which is the middle value?
maths.answer: 12 cm, 15 cm, 18 cm. The middle value is 15 cm.
maths.explain: A smaller number means the ruler fell a shorter way before the child caught it. So a smaller number is faster. In order from smallest: 12, 15, 18. The middle one is 15 cm.
maths.context: This is about the ruler-catch test in All Seven in Me. A grown-up drops a ruler and you catch it as fast as you can. The number at your thumb shows how far it fell before you sensed it and responded.
maths.why_maths: One try can be a fluke. Putting three tries in order and taking the middle one gives a fairer answer.

maths.problem: In the nature museum, a child found 3 living things, 9 once-alive things and 6 never-alive things. How many things did they find in all? How many more once-alive than never-alive things?
maths.answer: 18 things in all. 3 more once-alive things than never-alive things.
maths.explain: 3 + 9 + 6 = 18. Once alive was 9 and never alive was 6. 9 take away 6 is 3.
maths.context: This is about the nature museum box. You collected things on a walk and sorted them into three trays: alive, once alive and never alive.
maths.why_maths: A tally and a bar chart show at a glance which kind of thing is most common in a place, so we can ask why.

roots.context: We have been learning the seven signs that tell us something is alive. Now we ask what those signs tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Dry moong seeds can sit in a jar for months, doing almost nothing. Given water, they swell and sprout within a day or two. Boiled seeds look just the same, but never sprout. So you cannot tell a sleeping seed from a dead one by looking: only water can show it.
deep_truth.habit: We think 'alive' means 'doing something', like moving, eating or breathing. A dry seed breaks that habit: they are alive while doing almost nothing, and a boiled seed looks just the same but is dead.
deep_truth.evidence: In the seed test, dry seeds sprouted within a day or two of getting water, but boiled seeds with the same water never did. In the balloon test, dry yeast from a packet filled a balloon with gas soon after meeting warm sugar water.

three.who_am_i: You are a living body that keeps going without you trying. Even while you sleep, you breathe, grow and mend.
three.what_is_life: Life is not a thing you can hold in your hand. It is what a body does, or can still do: take in, change, give out, sense and make more.
three.what_is_this_world: Living and non-living things keep swapping their atoms. A tree takes in the carbon dioxide you breathe out and builds a mango with it. When you eat the mango, it becomes part of you.

roots.thread: A dry seed and a boiled seed are made of the same kinds of atoms, and they look the same. Only the dry seed can still grow. So life is not in the atoms alone, but in how they are put together and what they can do. Everything is conscious, down to the smallest particle. Feeding, growing, sensing and making more are the ways this awareness shows itself in a living body.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka tells his son Shvetaketu: if someone cuts this great tree at their root, or their middle, or their top, sap flows, but they live. Full of life, they stand drinking in water. But if life leaves one branch, that branch dries up. The body dies when life leaves it. Life itself does not die.
teachings.link: Uddalaka noticed the same signs we test: the tree drinks water and lives on after being cut, and a dead branch dries up. He then asked what life itself is, beyond the signs.

teachings.teaching: Jain teachings name six kinds of living beings: beings of earth, water, fire and air, plants, and beings that move about. All of them can be harmed, so we should harm none of them.
teachings.link: Jain thinkers drew the line of life far wider than science does. It shows that where we draw the line is partly our choice, and the choice changes how we treat the world.

teachings.source: J.C. Bose, Friday Evening Discourse at the Royal Institution, London, 10 May 1901
teachings.teaching: At the end of his talk, Bose said that his records of metals, plants and animals showed him one 'pervading unity' running through all things. He said that thinkers on the banks of the Ganga had taught this about three thousand years before.
teachings.link: Bose was a scientist who measured carefully. His measurements made him wonder whether living and non-living are two worlds, or one.

science.text: Seeds can stay alive for a very long time. A date palm seed about 2,000 years old, found at Masada in Israel, was sprouted in 2005 and grew into a tree.
How non-living chemicals first became living things, about 4,000 million years ago, is still unknown.

other_view.view: Most biologists say alive or not is a question of cells, energy and passing on instructions, not of awareness. Many would say that a seed, a wire or a stone is not aware at all. They say Bose's tired metal only looks like a living response. That is an honest view, and it is not ours.

practice.title: Seven signs, sitting still
practice.say: Let's sit very still together for one minute. Even now, you are doing the signs of life. Put a hand on your tummy and feel the breath going in and out. Now put two fingers on the side of your neck and feel your heartbeat. Listen for three sounds. That is sensing. Somewhere inside you, a hair is growing and a scratch is healing. You are not making any of it happen. It is just happening. Who is doing it?
practice.kid: Sit very still. Feel your breath go in and out. Feel your heartbeat. Listen for three sounds. Your body is doing life all by itself.

ask: If your breath goes into a tree, and the tree's mango becomes you, where do you stop and the tree begin?
Is a dry seed alive, asleep, or something in between?
Who decides what counts as alive: nature, or us?
Could something be a little bit alive?
roots.art: A child sitting cross-legged under a mango tree, eyes closed, with soft dotted lines showing breath flowing from the child to the leaves and back, and tiny atoms drifting between the child, the tree, a stone and a cloud.

how_we_found_out.story: For thousands of years, people believed that some living things start by themselves from non-living things. Maggots seemed to grow out of rotting meat, and mice out of old grain. This idea is called spontaneous generation. In 1668, Francesco Redi, an Italian doctor, put pieces of meat in jars. He left some jars open and covered others with fine cloth, so flies could not reach the meat. Flies landed on the open meat, and maggots appeared there. The covered meat rotted too, but no maggots grew on it. So the maggots hatched from eggs laid by flies. Still, many people thought tiny living things, too small to see, could start by themselves in soup. Around 1860, Louis Pasteur, in France, boiled soup in flasks with long, curved necks. Air could get in, but dust and tiny living things stuck in the bend. The soup stayed clear for months. When he snapped a neck off, the soup went cloudy within days. Today, life comes only from life.
how_we_found_out.who: Francesco Redi, an Italian doctor, and Louis Pasteur, a French scientist
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That living things such as maggots, mice and germs can start by themselves from meat, grain or soup. This is called spontaneous generation.
